second-polish-republic.t: Independent interwar Poland, reborn in 1918 after 123 years of partition, which defeated the Red Army in 1920 and fell to Germany and the USSR in 1939.
second-polish-republic.o: As the partitioning empires collapsed in November 1918, Jozef Pilsudski took power in Warsaw from the Regency Council of the Kingdom of Poland (1916-1918), and independence was proclaimed on 11 November. Poland's borders were settled by war: with the West Ukrainian People's Republic, with Germany in Greater Poland and Silesia, and with Soviet Russia, whose army was defeated at Warsaw in 1920.
second-polish-republic.r: The constitution of 1921 created a parliamentary republic, but after President Gabriel Narutowicz was murdered in 1922 and governments proved unstable, Pilsudski seized power in the May Coup of 1926. His Sanation regime ruled until 1939. About a third of the population were Ukrainians, Jews, Belarusians and Germans. The state built the port of Gdynia and the Central Industrial District.
second-polish-republic.e: Nazi Germany invaded on 1 September 1939 and the Soviet Union on 17 September, dividing the country. The government went into exile in France and London, and Poland was re-established in 1945 with new borders under communist rule.

side.t: Side, a Pamphylian port city with its own language and script, famous for its harbour and later its slave market.
side.o: Greeks from Cyme in Aeolis settled Side in the 7th century BCE on a peninsula of the Pamphylian coast. According to legend, they soon forgot Greek and spoke the local language, called Sidetic, written in a unique alphabet. The city's name means pomegranate.
side.r: Side was a self-governing port that thrived on trade and shipbuilding. It surrendered to Alexander of the Macedonian Empire in 333 BCE and came under the Ptolemaic Empire and the Seleucid Empire. In 190 BCE a Rhodian fleet defeated Hannibal off its shore.
side.e: In the 1st century BCE Side became a centre for Cilician pirates, who sold captives in its market. The Romans suppressed piracy, and in 25 BCE the city was included in the province of Galatia, flourishing under Rome.

swedish-wismar.t: Baltic port in Mecklenburg held by Sweden from the Peace of Westphalia until 1803, when it was pawned to Mecklenburg-Schwerin for a century.
swedish-wismar.o: Sweden occupied Wismar during the Thirty Years' War, and the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 gave it the town, the island of Poel and the district of Neukloster as an imperial fief. Wismar became one of Sweden's footholds on the southern Baltic, with Swedish Pomerania and Bremen-Verden.
swedish-wismar.r: Sweden turned Wismar into a heavily fortified naval base and placed there, from 1653, the Wismar Tribunal, the supreme court of appeal for all of Sweden's German possessions. The town kept its Hanseatic council and German law, while a Swedish governor commanded the garrison. Its trade suffered from the wars fought over it, and Danish and Prussian forces besieged it in 1675 and 1711-1716.
swedish-wismar.e: In 1803 Sweden pawned Wismar to the Duke of Mecklenburg-Schwerin for 1,250,000 riksdaler for 100 years, in the Treaty of Malmö. The loan was never repaid, and in 1903 Sweden renounced its rights, leaving Wismar to Germany.

sui-dynasty.t: The short dynasty that reunited China in 589, built the Grand Canal and laid the institutional foundations of the Tang.
sui-dynasty.o: Yang Jian, an aristocrat of mixed Han and Xianbei background and father-in-law of a Northern Zhou emperor, seized power as regent and took the throne in 581 as Emperor Wen. He built a new capital, Daxing, beside old Chang'an, absorbed Western Liang in 587 and conquered the Chen dynasty in 589.
sui-dynasty.r: Emperor Wen issued the Kaihuang Code, kept the equal-field land system and fubing militia, reformed local administration, took regular censuses and began recruiting officials by examination. He was a fervent patron of Buddhism. His son Emperor Yang built the eastern capital at Luoyang and linked the Yellow River and Yangtze with the Grand Canal, using vast forced labour.
sui-dynasty.e: Three failed invasions of Goguryeo between 612 and 614 drained manpower and sparked revolts across the empire. Emperor Yang withdrew to Jiangdu, where he was murdered in 618; Li Yuan, who had taken Chang'an, founded the Tang Dynasty, which kept most Sui institutions.

sultanate-of-angoche.t: A Swahili Muslim sultanate on the Mozambique coast that traded inland past the Portuguese and resisted colonial conquest until 1910.
sultanate-of-angoche.o: Angoche was founded on coastal islands in the late 15th century by Swahili settlers linked to Kilwa. It was already an established trading town when the Portuguese arrived, and it served as an alternative outlet for gold and ivory from the Zambezi valley, bypassing Portuguese-controlled Sofala and later Mozambique Island.
sultanate-of-angoche.r: The sultan ruled with a council of leading Swahili lineages, and the town was a centre of Islamic learning and Sufi brotherhoods for the coast. Trade in ivory and, in the 19th century, slaves for French and Brazilian buyers made it wealthy. Under Musa Mohamed Sahib Quanto in the 1860s Angoche expanded inland among the Makua.
sultanate-of-angoche.e: Portuguese forces occupied Angoche in 1861 and again in the 1890s, but resistance led by the Makua and Swahili continued. Sultan Farelay fought on until his capture in 1910, when the sultanate was absorbed into Portuguese Mozambique.

scalovians.t: Baltic people of the lower Neman river, between the Prussians and Lithuanians, conquered by the Teutonic Order in the 1270s.
scalovians.o: The Scalovians, or Skalvians, lived on both banks of the lower Neman in what is now the Kaliningrad region of Russia and western Lithuania. They were related to the Prussians and Curonians, and their territory lay on the river route linking the Baltic coast with inland Lithuania.
scalovians.r: They lived in farming and fishing communities defended by hillforts, including Ragnit on the Neman. Their position made them a buffer between the Teutonic Order and Lithuania, and they traded and intermarried with both Prussians and Lithuanians.
scalovians.e: The Teutonic Order campaigned against them from the 1270s, and by 1277 Scalovia was subdued. The Order built Ragnit castle in 1289 on the site of a Scalovian fort. Many Scalovians fled to Lithuania, and the region later became part of the area known as Lithuania Minor.

saguntum.t: The Iberian town of Arse, Rome's ally, whose siege and destruction by Hannibal in 219 BCE started the Second Punic War.
saguntum.o: Saguntum, called Arse by its inhabitants, grew in the 5th century BCE on a long rocky hill above the Palancia river, near the coast north of Valencia, within the Edetanian world. Greek writers wrongly believed it had been founded by settlers from Zakynthos.
saguntum.r: It was a prosperous Iberian town trading by sea with Greeks and Phoenicians and minting silver coins with the legend Arse. In the 220s BCE it made an alliance with Rome, though it lay south of the Ebro, the limit agreed between Rome and Hasdrubal in 226 BCE.
saguntum.e: In 219 BCE Hannibal besieged Saguntum for eight months and took it, and Rome's declaration of war on Carthage followed. The Scipios recaptured the town in 212 BCE and restored its people. Saguntum flourished as a Roman municipium, whose theatre and walls still survive.

state-of-buenos-aires.t: The province of Buenos Aires as a separate state, which broke away from the Argentine Confederation in 1852 and then reunited the nation on its terms.
state-of-buenos-aires.o: After Justo José de Urquiza overthrew Juan Manuel de Rosas at Caseros in 1852, he called a congress that would reduce Buenos Aires's control of customs revenue. On 11 September 1852 the province rebelled against him, rejected the national constitution of 1853 and in 1854 adopted its own constitution as the State of Buenos Aires.
state-of-buenos-aires.r: Buenos Aires kept the revenues of its port, the country's main source of income, while the Argentine Confederation governed from Paraná. Leaders such as Valentín Alsina and Bartolomé Mitre built schools, railways and a modern administration. Immigration and wool exports grew. Tension with the confederation led to tariff wars and armed conflict.
state-of-buenos-aires.e: Urquiza defeated Buenos Aires at Cepeda in 1859, and the Pact of San José de Flores brought it back into the confederation after constitutional amendments. Conflict resumed, and Mitre's victory at Pavón in 1861 led to national reunification under Buenos Aires's leadership as the Argentine Republic.

seljuk-emirate-of-aleppo.t: The Aleppo share of Tutush's realm under his son Ridwan, a weak state that paid tribute to Antioch and allied with the Assassins.
seljuk-emirate-of-aleppo.o: After Tutush I fell in battle in 1095, his son Ridwan secured Aleppo and northern Syria, while his brother Duqaq took Damascus. Their quarrels divided Muslim Syria at the moment the First Crusade arrived.
seljuk-emirate-of-aleppo.r: Ridwan lost territory to the Principality of Antioch and paid tribute to Tancred. Unpopular with the Sunni population, he relied on the Nizari Ismailis, allowing them a mission house in Aleppo and using their assassins against rivals. He also rejected a Seljuk-led counter-crusade in 1111 by closing the city's gates. After his death in 1113 his sons Alp Arslan al-Akhras and Sultan Shah were puppets of the eunuch Lu'lu' and other officers.
seljuk-emirate-of-aleppo.e: Threatened by the Franks, Aleppo's notables turned to outside protectors, and in 1117-1118 the city passed to the Artuqid Ilghazi, later part of the Artuqids of Mardin's sphere and then the Zengid dynasty.

second-taifa-of-mertola.t: A Sufi-led rebel state in the Algarve whose leader Ibn Qasi rose against the Almoravids and opened the way for the Almohads.
second-taifa-of-mertola.o: Ibn Qasi, a former tax official turned Sufi teacher, gathered disciples called the Muridun in the western Algarve. In 1144, as Almoravid rule weakened, his followers seized Mértola, and he proclaimed himself imam and mahdi.
second-taifa-of-mertola.r: The movement combined religious reform with rebellion against Almoravid taxes and jurists. Ibn Qasi was allied for a time with Ibn al-Mundhir of Silves and Sidray ibn Wazir of Beja, but they soon turned against him. He was among the first to appeal to the Almohads in Morocco, then sought support from Afonso I of Portugal.
second-taifa-of-mertola.e: His alliance with Portugal angered his own supporters, who killed him in Silves in 1151. Mértola passed to the Almohads, and his mystical writings were later studied by Ibn Arabi.

state-of-ba.t: The kingdom of the Ba warriors in the Three Gorges and Chongqing region, famed for salt springs and war dances, conquered by Qin with its neighbour Shu in 316 BCE.
state-of-ba.o: The Ba were peoples of the eastern Sichuan basin and the Three Gorges of the Yangtze. Tradition says their warriors fought alongside King Wu of Zhou against the Shang, singing and dancing as they advanced. A state led by a royal Ba lineage took shape in the 1st millennium BCE, its centre eventually at Jiangzhou in modern Chongqing.
state-of-ba.r: Ba controlled valuable brine springs and salt production along the Yangtze, which gave it wealth and influence over trade with the State of Chu. Its elite were buried in boat-shaped coffins and used distinctive willow-leaf bronze swords marked with Ba-Shu symbols that remain undeciphered. Relations with Chu alternated between alliance and war.
state-of-ba.e: Fighting between Ba and Ancient Shu gave the State of Qin its opportunity: in 316 BCE Qin armies conquered both and captured the king of Ba. Qin made the area Ba Commandery, while Ba elites kept local privileges. The name survives in the traditional term Ba-Shu for Sichuan and Chongqing culture.

sultanate-of-dahlak.t: An island sultanate in the Red Sea off Eritrea that controlled pearl fisheries and shipping between Egypt, Arabia and Ethiopia.
sultanate-of-dahlak.o: The Dahlak archipelago was drawn into the Islamic world early, serving as a place of exile under the Umayyads. By the 10th century a local Muslim dynasty ruled from Dahlak Kebir, the largest island, controlling the sea approaches to the Ethiopian coast and the port of Massawa.
sultanate-of-dahlak.r: The sultans grew rich from pearls, from customs on ships trading slaves, ivory and hides from the African mainland, and from their position on the route to Yemen and Egypt. Hundreds of Arabic tombstones from the 10th to 13th centuries record merchants, scholars and officials. The sultans often paid tribute to rulers in Yemen and dealt with Christian Ethiopia as both trade partner and rival.
sultanate-of-dahlak.e: The sultanate declined as trade shifted, and the Ottomans took Massawa and the islands in 1557, incorporating them into the Habesh Eyalet. Its cemeteries and cisterns on Dahlak Kebir are among the main medieval Islamic sites in the Horn of Africa.

sheikhdom-of-ras-al-khaimah.t: The seat of the Qawasim, a seafaring dynasty whose fleets challenged the British in the Gulf and who joined the UAE in 1972.
sheikhdom-of-ras-al-khaimah.o: The Qawasim, an Arab tribe on the northern coast of the Oman peninsula, established themselves at Ras al-Khaimah, near the old port of Julfar, in the early 18th century. They built a maritime power with branches on both shores of the Gulf, including Lingeh in Persia and Sharjah.
sheikhdom-of-ras-al-khaimah.r: The Qawasim lived from pearling, trade and sea warfare. Their attacks on shipping, partly linked to alliance with the Emirate of Diriyah, led the British to call the area the Pirate Coast. British expeditions in 1809 and 1819 destroyed their fleet and town, and the General Maritime Treaty of 1820 made the sheikhdom one of the Trucial States. It was ruled with Sharjah at times and separated permanently in 1921.
sheikhdom-of-ras-al-khaimah.e: Ras al-Khaimah stayed out of the United Arab Emirates at its founding in 1971, hoping for oil and a dispute over the Tunb islands, seized by Iran. It joined in February 1972 under Sheikh Saqr bin Muhammad Al Qasimi.

seha-river-land.t: The Seha River Land, a Hittite vassal kingdom of western Anatolia, caught between the Hittites and the Mycenaean Greeks.
seha-river-land.o: The Seha River Land formed part of the old Arzawa coalition in the valley of a western Anatolian river, probably the Bakırçay or Gediz. After the fall of Arzawa c. 1320 BCE, Mursili II confirmed Manapa-Tarhunta as its king under a Hittite treaty.
seha-river-land.r: Its rulers governed the river valley and, at times, the nearby island of Lazpa, probably Lesbos. A letter from Manapa-Tarhunta reports on events in Wilusa, and King Masturi married a sister of Muwatalli II of the Hittite Empire.
seha-river-land.e: Under Tudhaliya IV a king backed by Ahhiyawa rebelled and was defeated. The kingdom fades from the record with the collapse of the Hittite Empire c. 1180 BCE.

serbian-vojvodina.t: Self-proclaimed Serbian autonomous province in southern Hungary during the revolution of 1848, whose name lives on in today's Vojvodina.
serbian-vojvodina.o: As Hungary asserted its independence in spring 1848, Serbs of southern Hungary feared Magyarisation. A national assembly at Sremski Karlovci in May 1848 proclaimed the Serbian Vojvodina in Srem, Baranya, Bačka and Banat, elected Josif Rajačić patriarch and Colonel Stevan Šupljikac voivode, and set up a Main Board led by Đorđe Stratimirović.
serbian-vojvodina.r: The Vojvodina was a wartime administration rather than a settled state. Its forces, joined by volunteers from the Principality of Serbia, fought Hungarian revolutionary armies in bitter ethnic warfare across Bačka and Banat. The Serb leaders allied with the Habsburg court against Budapest, hoping for autonomy as a reward.
serbian-vojvodina.e: After Hungary's defeat in 1849, Vienna created the Voivodeship of Serbia and Banat of Temeschwar, an Austrian crown land run by German-speaking officials rather than by the Serbs. The name Vojvodina, however, became established for the region.

second-french-empire.t: Napoleon III's empire, which rebuilt Paris, built railways and a colonial empire, and collapsed after defeat by Prussia at Sedan in 1870.
second-french-empire.o: Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte, president of the French Second Republic, seized dictatorial power in a coup in December 1851. A plebiscite approved restoring the empire, and on 2 December 1852 he became Emperor Napoleon III.
second-french-empire.r: The early empire was authoritarian, with censorship and managed elections. Baron Haussmann rebuilt Paris with boulevards and sewers, and railways, banks and department stores expanded. France fought in the Crimea, helped unify Italy and gained Nice and Savoy in 1860, but the Mexican intervention failed. From 1860 the regime liberalised, becoming a parliamentary 'Liberal Empire' under Émile Ollivier in 1870.
second-french-empire.e: Provoked by Bismarck, France declared war on Prussia in July 1870. Napoleon III was captured at Sedan on 2 September, and two days later the French Third Republic was proclaimed in Paris. He died in exile in England in 1873.

sidicini.t: Small Oscan people of northern Campania whose appeal for help against the Samnites in 343 BCE set off Rome's first war with Samnium.
sidicini.o: The Sidicini lived around Teanum Sidicinum (modern Teano) in the hills between the Roccamonfina volcano and the Volturno, bordering the Aurunci and Campanians. They were an Oscan-speaking people, possibly related to the Samnites or the Ausones; their earlier history is unknown.
sidicini.r: Known mainly from Livy, they formed a small community centred on Teanum, which later issued its own coins in Oscan. In 343 BCE the Samnites attacked them; the Sidicini sought help from Capua, and Capua's appeal to Rome began the First Samnite War. They joined the Latins and Campanians against Rome in 340 BCE.
sidicini.e: Rome founded the Latin colony of Cales on land taken from the Sidicini and Aurunci in 334 BCE, ending their independence. Teanum Sidicinum became a Roman ally and later a municipium and colony.

second-turkic-khaganate.t: The revived Turkic empire of Mongolia, whose Orkhon inscriptions are the earliest surviving texts in a Turkic language.
second-turkic-khaganate.o: After fifty years of Tang rule, Ilterish Qaghan led a revolt in 682 and restored an independent Turkic state, with the support of the strategist Tonyukuk. His brother Qapaghan extended its power from Manchuria to the Syr Darya.
second-turkic-khaganate.r: The khagans ruled from the Otuken highlands in Mongolia, leading a confederation of Turkic tribes in wars against the Tang, the Kyrgyz and the Turgesh Khaganate. Under Bilge Qaghan and his brother, the general Kul Tegin, the state reached its cultural height. Their memorial stelae on the Orkhon River, written in the Old Turkic runic script, proclaim the duties of the khagan and warn the Turks against Chinese luxury.
second-turkic-khaganate.e: After Bilge Qaghan was poisoned in 734, succession struggles weakened the khaganate. In 744 an alliance of the Uyghurs, Basmyls and Karluks killed the last khagan, and the Uyghur Khaganate took its place.

swedish-livonia.t: Livonia under the Swedish crown, home to Riga, then the largest city of the Swedish realm, and to the university founded at Dorpat in 1632.
swedish-livonia.o: Gustav II Adolf captured Riga from Poland-Lithuania in 1621, and the Truce of Altmark in 1629 confirmed Swedish possession of most of the Duchy of Livonia, including southern Estonia and the island of Ösel after 1645. Latgale in the south-east stayed Polish.
swedish-livonia.r: A Swedish governor-general ruled from Riga, while the Baltic German knighthood kept its diet and Lutheran church. Gustav II Adolf founded the University of Dorpat in 1632, and the pastor Ernst Glück translated the Bible into Latvian in 1685-1689. Riga's exports of grain, flax and timber made it the busiest port in the Swedish empire. Charles XI's reduction of noble estates provoked the opposition of Johann Reinhold Patkul.
swedish-livonia.e: In the Great Northern War Russian troops besieged and took Riga in 1710 after a plague-stricken defence. The Treaty of Nystad in 1721 ceded Livonia to Russia, where it became the Governorate of Livonia. Later Latvians and Estonians remembered the Swedish period as 'the good Swedish times'.

sicilian-kingdom-of-1848.t: The independent Sicily proclaimed in the revolution of 1848, which deposed the Bourbons and held out for sixteen months.
sicilian-kingdom-of-1848.o: On 12 January 1848 Palermo rose against Ferdinand II of the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, one of the first revolutions of that year in Europe. The rebels took most of the island, revived the Sicilian constitution of 1812 and formed a government under the veteran admiral Ruggero Settimo.
sicilian-kingdom-of-1848.r: The Sicilian parliament declared the Bourbon dynasty deposed in April 1848 and in July offered the crown to Ferdinando, Duke of Genoa, son of Charles Albert of the Kingdom of Sardinia, who declined. The state had a government, parliament and army, but was divided between moderates and radicals and lacked foreign support.
sicilian-kingdom-of-1848.e: Ferdinand II's troops bombarded and took Messina in September 1848. The Bourbon offensive resumed in 1849, Catania fell in April and Palermo surrendered in May 1849, ending the kingdom.

second-brazilian-republic.t: The years of Getúlio Vargas's rise after the Revolution of 1930, when Brazil centralised power, gave women the vote and drifted towards dictatorship.
second-brazilian-republic.o: The Revolution of 1930 ended the First Brazilian Republic and installed Getúlio Vargas as head of a provisional government. He dissolved Congress and the state legislatures and appointed interventors to govern the states, breaking the power of the old oligarchies.
second-brazilian-republic.r: Vargas created a Ministry of Labour and began social legislation. São Paulo rose in the Constitutionalist Revolution of 1932, which was defeated. The constitution of 1934 gave women the vote and introduced corporatist representation, and Congress elected Vargas president. Politics polarised between the fascist-inspired Integralists and the left-wing National Liberation Alliance, which launched a failed communist uprising in 1935.
second-brazilian-republic.e: Citing an invented communist plot, the Cohen Plan, Vargas staged a coup on 10 November 1937, closing Congress and creating the authoritarian Estado Novo (Brazil). The 1934 constitution, Brazil's third, had lasted barely three years.

sallarid-emirate.t: A Daylamite dynasty that briefly ruled Azerbaijan and the eastern Caucasus in the 10th century, part of the so-called Iranian intermezzo between Arab and Turkic rule.
sallarid-emirate.o: The Sallarids, also called Musafirids, were a Daylamite family from Tarom in the mountains south of the Caspian. After the Sajid Emirate collapsed, Marzuban ibn Muhammad seized Azerbaijan in 941, taking Ardabil and Tabriz and extending his authority to Arran, Shirvan and Armenia.
sallarid-emirate.r: Marzuban ruled through Daylamite soldiers and local governors and drew tribute from Armenian and Albanian princes and the Shirvanshahs. The Sallarids were Ismaili-leaning Shiites ruling a largely Sunni population. In 943-944 Rus raiders seized Barda, and Marzuban besieged them until disease and his forces drove them out.
sallarid-emirate.e: Marzuban was captured by the Buyids in 948, and after his death in 957 his sons fought among themselves. Local Kurdish and Arab dynasties broke away, and around 981 the Rawwadid Emirate took over their remaining lands in Azerbaijan.

samanid-empire.t: A Persian dynasty ruling from Bukhara that revived New Persian as a literary language and made Transoxiana a centre of Islamic learning.
samanid-empire.o: The Samanids descended from Saman Khuda, a Persian landowner near Balkh who converted to Islam. In 819 the Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun gave his four grandsons governorships of Samarkand, Ferghana, Chach and Herat. Nasr ibn Ahmad unified their holdings, and his brother Isma'il ibn Ahmad defeated the Saffarids in 900, ruling Transoxiana and Khurasan as Abbasid governors.
samanid-empire.r: From Bukhara the emirs ran a sophisticated bureaucracy of divans modelled on the caliphate, with powerful viziers such as al-Bal'ami and al-Jayhani. Silver dirhams from Samanid mints flowed to Scandinavia through the Volga trade in slaves and furs. The court patronised the poet Rudaki and commissioned Persian translations, while scholars such as Ibn Sina and al-Razi worked under their rule. Sunni Islam spread to the Turkic steppe.
samanid-empire.e: Turkic slave generals gained power in the 10th century, and the Ghaznavid Empire took Khurasan. In 999 the Kara-Khanid Khanate captured Bukhara and ended the dynasty. The Samanids are remembered in Tajikistan as founders of Tajik statehood.

shang-dynasty.t: The first Chinese dynasty confirmed by its own writing, whose oracle-bone inscriptions and bronze vessels from Anyang open the recorded history of China.
shang-dynasty.o: According to tradition Tang of Shang overthrew Jie, last ruler of the Xia, around 1600 BCE. The Shang moved their capital several times, at sites such as Zhengzhou and Yanshi, until King Pan Geng settled at Yin, near modern Anyang in Henan, around 1300 BCE. From there the kings ruled the middle Yellow River plain.
shang-dynasty.r: The king was chief priest as well as war leader, consulting royal ancestors and the high god Di by cracking ox scapulae and turtle shells and carving the questions on them: the oldest substantial Chinese writing. Workshops cast massive bronze ritual vessels, chariots arrived from the steppe, and royal tombs held human sacrifices. The tomb of Fu Hao, a consort of King Wu Ding and a general, survived intact.
shang-dynasty.e: In 1046 BCE King Wu of Zhou defeated the last Shang king, Di Xin, at the Battle of Muye, and the Western Zhou took power. Shang descendants were given the State of Song to continue their ancestral sacrifices. The rediscovery of oracle bones in 1899 and excavations at Anyang from 1928 turned the Shang from legend into history.

shubria.t: Shubria, a Hurrian kingdom of the upper Tigris highlands that sheltered fugitives from Assyria until Esarhaddon conquered it.
shubria.o: Shubria lay in the mountains north of the upper Tigris, between Assyria and the Kingdom of Urartu. It emerged as a kingdom after the Late Bronze Age, inhabited by Hurrian speakers whose culture survived longer there than elsewhere.
shubria.r: Its kings, ruling from Uppumu, played Assyria and Urartu against each other. Shubria was known as a refuge where fugitives, deserters and escaped slaves from the Assyrian Empire could find asylum, a practice its kings defended.
shubria.e: When King Ik-Teshub refused to hand over fugitives, Esarhaddon of the Assyrian Empire captured Uppumu in 673 BCE and annexed Shubria, recording the campaign in a letter to the god Ashur.

swiss-confederation.t: Modern Switzerland, a federal state of cantons that became a model of neutrality, direct democracy and multilingual government.
swiss-confederation.o: Napoleon's Act of Mediation of 1803 replaced the centralised Helvetic Republic with a confederation of 19 cantons, including new cantons such as Vaud, Aargau and Ticino formed from former subject lands. After Napoleon's fall the Federal Treaty of 1815 and the Congress of Vienna added Geneva, Valais and Neuchâtel and recognised Swiss neutrality.
swiss-confederation.r: Tensions between liberal Protestant and conservative Catholic cantons led to the Sonderbund War of 1847. The federal constitution of 1848 created a federal state with a two-chamber parliament and a seven-member Federal Council, with Bern as federal city. Referendums and popular initiatives were added in 1874 and 1891. Industry, banking and tourism grew, and German, French, Italian and Romansh are national languages.
swiss-confederation.e: Switzerland stayed neutral in both world wars. Women gained the federal vote only in 1971, and the canton of Jura was created in 1979. It joined the United Nations in 2002 but remains outside the European Union.

samnite-league.t: Confederation of the Oscan-speaking peoples of the southern Apennines, Rome's toughest opponent in Italy during three Samnite Wars.
samnite-league.o: The Samnites lived in the mountains of modern Molise and inland Campania. They believed they descended from Sabines who had migrated south in a 'sacred spring'. By the 5th century BCE they had formed a confederation of four peoples, the Pentri, Caraceni, Caudini and Hirpini, with Bovianum as a main centre.
samnite-league.r: Each people (touto) was governed by an elected magistrate, the meddix tuticus, and the league acted together in war. Society was rural, living in villages and hill forts. The great sanctuary at Pietrabbondante, with its temple and theatre, was a federal centre. Samnite warriors were famed for their armour, and their expansion carried Oscan speech into Campania, Lucania and Bruttium.
samnite-league.e: Rome fought three Samnite Wars from 343 to 290 BCE. The Samnites trapped a Roman army at the Caudine Forks in 321 BCE but lost at Sentinum in 295 BCE and accepted Roman alliance in 290 BCE. They later backed Pyrrhus and Hannibal, and Sulla crushed them at the Colline Gate in 82 BCE.

sambians.t: Prussian people of the Sambian peninsula, the world's richest source of Baltic amber, whose conquest in 1255 led to the founding of Königsberg.
sambians.o: The Sambians lived on the Sambian peninsula between the Vistula and Curonian lagoons, in today's Kaliningrad region. Their amber had reached the Roman world, and in the Viking Age Scandinavian traders settled at Wiskiauten nearby. Adam of Bremen in the 11th century described the Sambians as humane people with much fur.
sambians.r: Sambia was the most populous and wealthy Prussian land, with nobles holding fortified seats and a strong warrior class. Amber, furs and slaves were traded across the Baltic. The Sambians kept the Prussian pagan religion and resisted Danish and Polish missions.
sambians.e: In 1255 a crusade led by King Ottokar II of Bohemia subdued Sambia, and the Teutonic Order founded Königsberg, named in his honour. The Sambians rose again from 1260 under Glande but were defeated. Many nobles joined the Order's service, and their land became Order territory and the Bishopric of Samland.

serbian-hungarian-baranya-baja-republic.t: Leftist republic proclaimed in Pécs in 1921 as Yugoslav troops prepared to hand the region back to Horthy's Hungary.
serbian-hungarian-baranya-baja-republic.o: Yugoslav forces occupied Pécs and the coal-mining region of Baranya in November 1918. The area became a refuge for Hungarian socialists, communists and liberals fleeing the White Terror. When the Treaty of Trianon returned the area to Hungary, they proclaimed the Serbian-Hungarian Baranya-Baja Republic on 14 August 1921, with the painter Petar Dobrović as president.
serbian-hungarian-baranya-baja-republic.r: The republic was a last-minute attempt to stop the return of Horthy's regime, and hoped either for independence or union with Yugoslavia. It had a provisional government and relied on miners' support, but had no means of defence once Yugoslav troops left.
serbian-hungarian-baranya-baja-republic.e: Hungarian troops entered Pécs on 21 and 22 August 1921, ending the republic after about a week. Thousands of its supporters fled to the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, and the region returned to the Kingdom of Hungary (1920-1946).

sican.t: A theocratic culture of Peru's north coast, centred on the pyramids of Batán Grande, that dominated Andean goldworking and trade in arsenical bronze.
sican.o: The Sicán culture, also called Lambayeque, emerged around 750 in the La Leche and Lambayeque valleys, in the former territory of the Moche. A legend recorded by the Spanish tells of Naymlap, who arrived by sea with a fleet of balsa rafts and founded a dynasty there.
sican.r: Middle Sicán, about 900 to 1100, was ruled from the Sicán Precinct at Batán Grande, with large adobe pyramids such as Huaca Loro. Elite tombs contained tonnes of grave goods, including gold masks and arsenical copper. Sicán produced arsenical bronze on a large scale and used naipes, small copper axe-shaped objects, possibly as a form of currency. Trade reached Ecuador for spondylus shell. Its art centred on the Sicán Lord, a figure with winged eyes.
sican.e: Around 1100 a severe drought followed by El Niño floods led to the burning and abandonment of Batán Grande. Late Sicán continued at Túcume until the region was conquered by the Kingdom of Chimor around 1375.

sulayhid-dynasty.t: An Isma'ili dynasty that united Yemen under the Fatimid banner and is remembered for Queen Arwa, one of the few women to rule in medieval Islam.
sulayhid-dynasty.o: Ali ibn Muhammad al-Sulayhi, a judge's son and Isma'ili missionary for the Fatimid Caliphate, rose in revolt in the Haraz mountains in 1047. Within two decades he had taken Sanaa, Zabid and Aden and brought most of Yemen under his rule, recognising the Fatimid caliph in Cairo.
sulayhid-dynasty.r: The Sulayhids spread the Fatimid mission to Oman and western India. After Ali was killed by the Najahid dynasty, power passed to his son al-Mukarram Ahmad and then to Ahmad's wife, Arwa bint Ahmad, who governed from Dhu Jibla for some fifty years, built its great mosque and was given authority over the Fatimid mission in Yemen. Governors such as the Zurayids ruled Aden for them.
sulayhid-dynasty.e: When the Fatimids split over succession in 1130, Arwa backed the infant al-Tayyib, founding the Tayyibi branch of Isma'ilism. After her death in 1138 the state broke apart among the Zurayid dynasty, the Hamdanid sultanate of Yemen and others. Tayyibi leadership later moved to India, where the Bohras continue it.

state-of-aleppo.t: The French-created state of northern Syria around Aleppo, which existed for four years before being merged into the State of Syria.
state-of-aleppo.o: Following the defeat of the Arab Kingdom of Syria, the French high commissioner Henri Gouraud created the State of Aleppo in September 1920. It covered northern Syria and the Euphrates valley and included the Sanjak of Alexandretta, which had a special regime.
state-of-aleppo.r: The state was governed by local notables under French supervision; its first governor was Kamil Pasha al-Qudsi. Aleppo's merchants suffered from the new borders, which cut the city off from its Anatolian hinterland after the 1921 Treaty of Ankara with Turkey. In 1922 the state joined the Syrian Federation.
state-of-aleppo.e: At the end of 1924 France merged the states of Aleppo and Damascus into the State of Syria, effective January 1925, while Alexandretta kept its autonomy.

shilluk-kingdom.t: A kingdom of the Shilluk people on the White Nile, famous for its sacred kingship centred on the reth and the founder-hero Nyikang.
shilluk-kingdom.o: According to Shilluk tradition, the kingdom was founded by Nyikang, who led his people north along the White Nile and settled them on its west bank. Historians date the establishment of the kingship to around the late 15th century, with Fashoda becoming the royal centre.
shilluk-kingdom.r: The reth was a sacred king, believed to embody the spirit of Nyikang; his health was linked to the wellbeing of the land, a case made famous by James Frazer and E. E. Evans-Pritchard. Settlements were dense along the river, living from sorghum, cattle and fishing. Shilluk canoe fleets raided as far north as the Funj Sultanate.
shilluk-kingdom.e: In the 19th century slave traders and the Turco-Egyptian Sudan broke Shilluk power; Egyptian forces subdued the kingdom around 1861. Fashoda later gave its name to the Anglo-French crisis of 1898. The reth survives today as a traditional ruler in South Sudan.

state-of-deng.t: A small kingdom of the Man clan on the Han River, older than the Zhou, whose marriage ties with Chu did not save it from being swallowed by that rising power in 678 BCE.
state-of-deng.o: Deng appears in Shang oracle-bone inscriptions and survived the Zhou conquest as a minor state ruled by the Man clan, centred near modern Xiangyang in Hubei and the Nanyang basin of Henan. It lay on the route between the Central Plain and the middle Yangtze.
state-of-deng.r: Little is recorded of its institutions. Deng is known mainly through the Zuo zhuan, which notes marriages between its ruling house and the kings of Chu: Deng Man was the wife of King Wu of Chu and mother of King Wen. Bronze vessels inscribed with the name of Deng rulers have been found in Hubei and Henan.
state-of-deng.e: When King Wen of Chu passed through Deng on campaign, the Marquis of Deng refused his advisers' urging to kill his visiting nephew. Chu attacked Deng soon afterwards and annexed it in 678 BCE, an early step in the State of Chu's expansion northwards.

segusiavi.t: Gallic people of the Forez and Lyonnais on whose land Rome founded Lyon, the future capital of the Three Gauls.
segusiavi.o: The Segusiavi lived between the Loire and the Rhône, in the plains of the Forez and the hills west of the Saône. Caesar describes them as the first people beyond the Rhône outside the Roman Province and as clients of the Aedui.
segusiavi.r: Few details survive. Their territory commanded the crossing of the Saône and Rhône at the hill of Fourvière, a strategic point for trade between the Mediterranean and central Gaul.
segusiavi.e: They joined the revolt of 52 BCE with the Aedui. In 43 BCE the colony of Lugdunum (Lyon) was founded on their land, and their own chief town became Forum Segusiavorum (Feurs). Their name survives in the Forez region.

smyrna-zone.t: The Greek-administered zone around Smyrna after the First World War, which ended in the destruction of the city in 1922.
smyrna-zone.o: With the approval of the Allies, Greek troops landed at Smyrna on 15 May 1919, ostensibly to protect the large Greek Orthodox population. The landing was marred by killings of Turks and helped ignite the Turkish national movement. The Treaty of Sevres of 1920 placed the zone under Greek administration, with a plebiscite on union with Greece after five years.
smyrna-zone.r: The High Commissioner Aristeidis Stergiadis ran the zone and tried, with mixed success, to treat Muslims and Christians equally. A Greek university, the Ionian University, was planned under the mathematician Constantin Caratheodory. The zone served as the base for the Greek army's offensives deep into Anatolia in 1920-1921.
smyrna-zone.e: After the Greek defeat at Dumlupinar in August 1922, Turkish forces entered Smyrna on 9 September. A great fire destroyed the Greek and Armenian quarters, and the Christian population fled. The 1923 Treaty of Lausanne and population exchange confirmed the city's place in the Republic of Turkey.

state-of-grao-para-and-rio-negro.t: A short-lived Portuguese administrative state covering the Amazon basin, governed from Belém after the division of Grão-Pará and Maranhão.
state-of-grao-para-and-rio-negro.o: In 1772 the State of Grão-Pará and Maranhão was split in two. The western part, comprising the Captaincy of Grão-Pará and the Captaincy of São José do Rio Negro, created in 1755 with its seat at Barcelos, became the State of Grão-Pará and Rio Negro, governed from Belém.
state-of-grao-para-and-rio-negro.r: The state covered most of the Brazilian Amazon. Its economy relied on forest products such as cacao, cloves and sarsaparilla gathered by indigenous workers under the Directorate system, and on trade through Belém with Lisbon. Portuguese forts along the Rio Negro and Rio Branco guarded the frontier with Spanish territories.
state-of-grao-para-and-rio-negro.e: The separate state was short-lived; from the mid-1770s its captaincies were increasingly brought under the general government of Brazil. Grão-Pará remained loyal to Lisbon at independence and joined the Empire of Brazil only in 1823. The Cabanagem revolt shook the region from 1835 to 1840.

sophene.t: Sophene, an Armenian kingdom in the upper Euphrates valley, ruled by a branch of the Orontid dynasty until Tigranes the Great absorbed it.
sophene.o: Sophene lay west of the Tigris sources around modern Elazığ, the old land of Isuwa. In the 3rd century BCE an Orontid prince, Arsames, ruled it and founded Arsamosata. It was part of the wider Armenian world of the Kingdom of Armenia (Orontid), though often under Seleucid overlordship.
sophene.r: Its kings controlled important crossings of the Euphrates and Tigris and the routes between Anatolia and Mesopotamia. Antiochus III appointed Zariadres as governor; after Rome defeated Antiochus in 189 BCE, Zariadres declared himself king. The court mixed Iranian and Greek traditions.
sophene.e: Around 95 BCE Tigranes the Great of the Kingdom of Armenia (Artaxiad) deposed its last king, Artanes, and annexed Sophene, uniting Armenia.

saadi-sultanate.t: The sharifian dynasty that drove the Portuguese from much of Morocco, defeated them at the Battle of the Three Kings and conquered Songhai.
saadi-sultanate.o: The Saadis were a sharifian family from the Draa valley who rose in 1510 under Muhammad al-Qa'im as leaders of holy war against Portuguese Morocco. They took Marrakesh from the Hintata emirate around 1525, captured Agadir in 1541 and Fez from the Wattasid Sultanate in 1549, uniting Morocco under Muhammad al-Shaykh.
saadi-sultanate.r: The Saadis kept Morocco free of Ottoman control and built an army with firearms and renegades. In 1578 they crushed King Sebastian of Portugal at Alcácer Quibir. Ahmad al-Mansur grew rich from sugar and Saharan gold, sent an army that destroyed the Songhai Empire in 1591, and built the El Badi palace in Marrakesh.
saadi-sultanate.e: After al-Mansur's death in 1603 his sons fought a long civil war, splitting the realm between Fez and Marrakesh. Local powers such as the Dila'iyya and the Republic of Salé rose, and the last Saadi was killed in 1659. The Alaouite Sultanate inherited Morocco.

state-of-grao-para-and-maranhao.t: Pombal's reorganised Amazon colony, ruled from Belém, where Jesuit control of indigenous peoples was ended and a monopoly company brought enslaved Africans.
state-of-grao-para-and-maranhao.o: In 1751 the Marquis of Pombal reorganised the State of Maranhão as the State of Grão-Pará and Maranhão, moving its capital from São Luís to Belém. His brother Francisco Xavier de Mendonça Furtado became governor, charged with mapping the borders agreed with Spain in the Treaty of Madrid and asserting royal power in the Amazon.
state-of-grao-para-and-maranhao.r: Mendonça Furtado clashed with the Jesuits, who controlled indigenous villages and labour. In 1755 a law freed indigenous people from missionary rule, and from 1757 the Directorate placed their villages under lay directors and promoted Portuguese over the língua geral. The Jesuits were expelled in 1759. The General Company of Grão-Pará and Maranhão, founded in 1755, held a trade monopoly and imported enslaved Africans for cotton and rice plantations.
state-of-grao-para-and-maranhao.e: In 1772 the state was divided into the State of Grão-Pará and Rio Negro and the State of Maranhão and Piauí. The trading company lost its monopoly in 1778. Its policies towards indigenous peoples shaped the Amazon for decades, and Belém remained the region's capital.

state-of-rui.t: A Ji-clan state on the Yellow River bend whose rich cemetery at Liangdai and outspoken minister Rui Liangfu make it one of the better-known minor Zhou states.
state-of-rui.o: Rui was a Western Zhou fief held by a branch of the royal Ji clan, its lords ranked as earls. It lay along the Yellow River where it divides Shaanxi from Shanxi, near modern Ruicheng and later at Liangdai village by Hancheng.
state-of-rui.r: Earl Rui Liangfu served at the royal court and is remembered for warning King Li of Zhou against monopolising the kingdom's resources. In 709 BCE Earl Wan of Rui was driven out by his mother, Rui Jiang, and the states of Qin and Jin intervened. The Liangdai cemetery, excavated from 2005, yielded fine jades and gold ornaments.
state-of-rui.e: Wedged between rising Qin and Jin, Rui was annexed by the State of Qin in 640 BCE as Qin pushed east towards the Yellow River.

shapsugs.t: The largest of the self-governing Circassian peoples on the Black Sea coast, who overthrew their nobility and fought Russia until 1864.
shapsugs.o: The Shapsugs lived along the Black Sea coast and inland hills between the Natukhaj and the Ubykhs, around modern Tuapse, and on the northern slopes towards the Kuban. They emerged as a distinct Adyghe community of Circassia by the 17th century; earlier history is not separately recorded.
shapsugs.r: In the late 18th century Shapsug commoners rose against their nobles and defeated them and their Bzhedugh allies at Bziyuqo in 1796. Afterwards they were governed by assemblies of elders and representatives of free households. They farmed, herded and traded with Ottoman ships. In the 1840s and 1850s they joined the assemblies that coordinated Circassian resistance.
shapsugs.e: The Russian Empire conquered their territory in 1864, and most Shapsugs were expelled to the Ottoman Empire. A small community remained near Tuapse and Lazarevskoye, the only Circassians left on the Black Sea coast.

sidon.t: Sidon, one of the oldest Phoenician cities, whose kings led the Persian navy and whose name long stood for all Phoenicians.
sidon.o: Sidon stood on a promontory with offshore islets forming a harbour on the southern Lebanese coast. Inhabited since prehistory, it was a Canaanite port in the Amarna age, and in Homer and the Bible Sidonians means Phoenicians in general, a sign of its early prestige.
sidon.r: Its kings ruled a merchant city famous for glass and purple cloth, and honoured the healing god Eshmun at a great sanctuary outside the city. Under the Achaemenid Empire Sidon was the leading Phoenician city and supplied the core of the Persian fleet; the inscribed sarcophagus of Eshmunazar II survives.
sidon.e: Esarhaddon of the Assyrian Empire razed the city in 677 BCE, and Artaxerxes III burned it again after King Tennes rebelled. In 332 BCE Sidon opened its gates to Alexander of the Macedonian Empire, who installed Abdalonymus as king, ending its independent history.

syrian-federation.t: A short-lived federation of the French-created Syrian states, a step towards reuniting Syria under the mandate.
syrian-federation.o: In June 1922 the French high commissioner Henri Gouraud united the State of Damascus, the State of Aleppo and the Alawite State in a federation, a partial response to nationalist demands for unity.
syrian-federation.r: A federal council of delegates from the three states, under the presidency of Subhi Barakat, handled common affairs, while each state kept its own government and French officials held real power. The capital alternated between Aleppo and Damascus. The federation had a single budget, customs and currency, but nationalists criticised it as a French device that kept Lebanon, the Jabal Druze and Alexandretta apart from Syria. The Alawite State withdrew at the start of 1925.
syrian-federation.e: At the end of 1924 France dissolved the federation, merging Damascus and Aleppo into the State of Syria from January 1925.

sultanate-of-lahej.t: The Abdali sultanate north of Aden, which lost Aden to Britain in 1839 but remained the leading state of the Aden hinterland.
sultanate-of-lahej.o: The Abdali tribe held the fertile Lahej oasis north of Aden. Around 1728, under Sultan Fadl ibn Ali, they rejected the authority of the Qasimid State and founded an independent sultanate, which also took control of the port of Aden.
sultanate-of-lahej.r: Lahej lived on irrigated agriculture and the trade passing between Aden and the interior. In 1839 the British East India Company seized Aden from Sultan Muhsin ibn Fadl, creating the Aden Settlement, and Lahej became the most important of the protected states around it. Ottoman forces occupied Lahej in 1915-1918. The sultanate's court was a centre of poetry and song, notably under Ahmad Fadl al-Qumandan.
sultanate-of-lahej.e: Britain deposed Sultan Ali ibn Abd al-Karim in 1958 for his nationalist contacts. Lahej joined the Federation of South Arabia, and in 1967 the National Liberation Front took over, abolishing the sultanate within South Yemen.

second-taifa-of-niebla.t: Niebla's brief independence under Yusuf al-Bitruji during the 1140s revolts against the Almoravids in the far west of al-Andalus.
second-taifa-of-niebla.o: In 1145 Yusuf ibn Ahmad al-Bitruji, a local leader, took control of the walled town of Niebla on the Tinto river, as the revolt begun by Ibn Qasi in the Algarve spread through the south-west.
second-taifa-of-niebla.r: Known only from brief chronicle references, Niebla was one of several small regimes that rose and fell in quick succession. Its ruler was drawn into conflicts with Almoravid loyalists in Seville and with neighbouring rebels.
second-taifa-of-niebla.e: Niebla submitted to the Almohads around 1150. A century later it became independent again as the Third Taifa of Niebla.

siphnos.t: Cycladic island that grew briefly rich on gold and silver mines and built a celebrated treasury at Delphi.
siphnos.o: Siphnos, in the western Cyclades, was settled by Ionian Greeks from Athens in the early Iron Age. Its silver and gold deposits, worked since the Bronze Age, made it in the 6th century BCE the richest island of the Aegean, according to Herodotus.
siphnos.r: Siphnians shared their mining income as citizens and gave a tithe to Delphi, where they built the Siphnian Treasury c. 525 BCE, with its famous sculpted frieze. Exiles from Samos extorted a hundred talents from the island c. 524 BCE. Siphnos later sent a ship to Salamis and paid tribute in the Delian League.
siphnos.e: The mines failed, flooded by the sea, which legend blamed on the Siphnians cheating Apollo of his tithe. The island remained a modest community known for its pottery under Hellenistic powers and Rome, losing independence by 146 BCE.

silvanectes.t: Small Gallic people of the forests north of Paris whose town Augustomagus became Senlis.
silvanectes.o: The Silvanectes are not named by Caesar and were probably part of the Suessiones during the conquest. Pliny and Ptolemy record them as a separate people between the Parisii, Bellovaci and Suessiones.
silvanectes.r: Their name has been linked to the forests of the Oise, but nothing is recorded of their society.
silvanectes.e: Under Rome they formed a civitas with Augustomagus (Senlis) as its chief town. It became a bishopric and in 987 the assembly at Senlis elected Hugh Capet king, founding the Kingdom of France.

sultanate-of-ouargla.t: An oasis sultanate in the Algerian Sahara, ruling Ouargla's palm groves at a crossroads of caravan routes between the Maghreb and the Sahel.
sultanate-of-ouargla.o: Ouargla had been an Ibadi and trading centre since the early Middle Ages, near the ruined city of Sedrata. A local sultanate is attested from around 1500, when chroniclers such as Leo Africanus describe the town as a wealthy caravan stop with its own ruler.
sultanate-of-ouargla.r: The sultans had limited power, mediating between the town's factions, the surrounding nomadic tribes such as the Chaamba, and Berber-speaking oasis farmers. The economy rested on date palms, irrigation and trade in slaves, gold and goods between the Mediterranean and the Sahel. Ouargla paid tribute at times to the Regency of Algiers and competed with the Sultanate of Touggourt.
sultanate-of-ouargla.e: The French extended their influence in the 1850s, and French Algeria occupied Ouargla in 1872, ending the sultanate. The town later became the centre of the Algerian oil industry.

serbia-and-montenegro.t: Loose union of Serbia and Montenegro that replaced the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and ended when Montenegro voted for independence.
serbia-and-montenegro.o: By 2001 Montenegro's government sought independence from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. To avoid a sudden break, the European Union, through Javier Solana, brokered the Belgrade Agreement of 2002. A Constitutional Charter adopted on 4 February 2003 turned the federation into the State Union of Serbia and Montenegro, with Belgrade as its seat.
serbia-and-montenegro.r: The union had a single-chamber parliament, a president, Svetozar Marović, and a small council of ministers handling foreign affairs, defence and human rights. Otherwise the two republics ran their own affairs: Montenegro used the euro and Serbia the dinar, with separate customs systems. The charter allowed either member to hold an independence referendum after three years.
serbia-and-montenegro.e: In a referendum on 21 May 2006, 55.5 percent of Montenegrin voters chose independence, just above the 55 percent threshold set by the EU. Montenegro declared independence on 3 June 2006, and Serbia became the union's legal successor.

sogn.t: Petty kingdom around the Sognefjord, Norway's longest fjord, absorbed into Harald Fairhair's realm in the late 9th century.
sogn.o: Sogn, the land around the great Sognefjord in western Norway, appears in the sagas as one of the small kingdoms of the Viking Age. Rich graves along the fjord show a prosperous elite in the Iron Age, but its rulers are known only from late Icelandic tradition.
sogn.r: Its people farmed the fjord slopes, raised livestock in mountain pastures and traded along the coast and over the mountains to eastern Norway. The site of the Gulating, the great law assembly of western Norway, lay at Gulen near the mouth of the fjord, and the district later belonged to its law province.
sogn.e: The sagas say Harald Fairhair took Sogn during his conquest of the west coast and placed it under one of his earls. It became part of the Kingdom of Norway; in the Middle Ages Sogn was known for its stave churches, including Urnes, now a World Heritage Site.

state-of-maranhao-and-piaui.t: A short-lived Portuguese administrative state on Brazil's northern coast, governed from São Luís after the division of Grão-Pará and Maranhão in 1772.
state-of-maranhao-and-piaui.o: When the State of Grão-Pará and Maranhão was divided in 1772, the eastern part, made up of the captaincies of Maranhão and Piauí, became the State of Maranhão and Piauí, with its capital at São Luís.
state-of-maranhao-and-piaui.r: Maranhão grew cotton and rice for export on plantations worked by enslaved Africans, many imported by the General Company of Grão-Pará and Maranhão, and São Luís prospered as a port. Piauí, with its capital at Oeiras, was a land of cattle ranches supplying meat to the northeast. Little is known of the state's separate administration.
state-of-maranhao-and-piaui.e: The separate state was soon merged back into the general administration of Brazil, and its captaincies became provinces after 1821. Maranhão stayed loyal to Portugal at independence and joined the Empire of Brazil only in 1823. Piauí and Maranhão are today states of Brazil.

samos-empire.t: The first known Slavic political union, led by the Frankish merchant Samo, which threw off Avar rule and defeated a Frankish king.
samos-empire.o: Around 623 the Slavs of central Europe, called Wends in the Chronicle of Fredegar, rebelled against their Avar overlords. Samo, a Frankish merchant trading with them, fought so well that they chose him as king. The location of his realm is debated, but it probably covered Bohemia, Moravia, parts of Slovakia and Lower Austria.
samos-empire.r: Fredegar, the only substantial source, reports that Samo ruled for 35 years, had twelve Slavic wives and won every battle against the Avars. In 631 a dispute over murdered Frankish merchants led King Dagobert I to invade; Samo defeated the Franks at Wogastisburg, and the Sorb prince Dervan then joined him.
samos-empire.e: After Samo's death around 658 his union seems to have dissolved, and nothing more is heard of it; the Avars regained influence in the region. It is remembered as a forerunner of later Slavic states such as Great Moravia and Carantania, though no direct continuity is known.

sestos.t: Greek city on the European shore of the Hellespont, key to the grain route, whose capture by Athens in 478 BCE closes Herodotus's Histories.
sestos.o: Sestos was founded by Aeolian settlers from Lesbos on the Thracian Chersonese, at the narrows of the Hellespont opposite Abydos. Its harbour and position made it the main crossing point from Asia into Europe.
sestos.r: Sestos lay near the site of Xerxes's bridges in 480 BCE. In 479 to 478 BCE the Athenians under Xanthippus besieged and took it, the episode that ends Herodotus's Histories. It became a key Athenian base for protecting the Black Sea grain route and paid tribute in the Delian League. Greek legend made it the home of Hero, beloved of Leander.
sestos.e: After the Athenian defeat at nearby Aegospotami in 405 BCE, Sestos passed to Sparta, then back to Athens and later to Macedonian and Hellenistic rulers. It came under Roman control by 146 BCE.

scordisci.t: Celtic people at the meeting of the Sava and Danube who founded Singidunum, modern Belgrade, and harried Roman Macedonia for two centuries.
scordisci.o: After the Celtic invasion of Greece under Brennus failed in 279 BCE, survivors settled at the confluence of the Sava and Danube. There they merged with local Illyrian and Thracian peoples and formed the Scordisci, with strongholds at Singidunum (Belgrade) and Taurunum (Zemun).
scordisci.r: A warrior aristocracy ruled over a mixed population, dominating the middle Danube from fortified oppida. They minted coins, traded along the river and raided south. In 114 BCE they destroyed a Roman army under Gaius Porcius Cato in Macedonia, and wars with Rome followed for decades. The Dacian king Burebista defeated them in the mid-1st century BCE.
scordisci.e: Tiberius subdued the Scordisci during his Pannonian campaigns of 12–9 BCE, and they became allies of Rome. By the early 1st century CE they were absorbed into the provinces of Pannonia and Moesia, and the name Singidunum survived as a Roman legionary base.

saaremaa.t: Estonia's largest island and its seafaring people, the Oeselians, feared raiders of the Baltic who held out against the crusaders until 1227.
saaremaa.o: Saaremaa, known to Germans and Scandinavians as Ösel, was densely settled in the Iron Age, with strong hillforts such as Valjala and Kaarma. Its inhabitants, the Oeselians, appear in Norse sagas and in Henry of Livonia's chronicle as skilled sailors and pirates.
saaremaa.r: Each parish was led by elders, who joined together for raids and defence. The Oeselians attacked the coasts of Denmark and Sweden and, in 1220, destroyed a Swedish garrison at Lihula on the mainland. They also traded across the Baltic and worshipped a god Henry calls Tharapita.
saaremaa.e: In early 1227 a crusader army crossed the frozen sea and took Valjala, forcing the islanders to accept baptism. The island was divided between the Bishopric of Ösel-Wiek and the Livonian Order. Its people rebelled repeatedly, notably in 1343, and Saaremaa later passed to Danish Ösel.

state-of-xing.t: A Zhou fief in southern Hebei founded by a son of the Duke of Zhou, rescued from Di raiders by Qi and finally destroyed by its kinsmen of Wey.
state-of-xing.o: Xing was granted early in the Western Zhou to a son of the Duke of Zhou, a member of the royal Ji clan, as a northern outpost near modern Xingtai in Hebei. Inscribed bronzes such as the Mai vessels record its rulers' audiences with the Zhou king.
state-of-xing.r: As a frontier state Xing guarded the Zhou world against the Di peoples of the Taihang uplands. Little is known of its internal life beyond the bronzes and brief entries in the Zuo zhuan, which show a typical Zhou aristocratic state organised around its ruling lineage and ancestral temple.
state-of-xing.e: Di attacks overran Xing in the 660s BCE. Duke Huan of Qi led a coalition to rescue it and resettled its people at Yiyi in 659 BCE. Weakened, Xing was annexed in 635 BCE by the State of Wey, a fellow Ji-clan state, which was criticised for destroying kin.

state-of-sui.t: A Ji-clan state in Hubei, now identified with the Zeng of the bronzes, whose Marquis Yi was buried with the most famous set of chime bells in China.
state-of-sui.o: Sui was founded early in the Western Zhou by a branch of the royal Ji clan at Suizhou in northern Hubei, guarding the corridor to the copper mines of the middle Yangtze. Excavated bronzes call the state Zeng, and most scholars now treat Sui and Zeng as the same state.
state-of-sui.r: In the 8th and 7th centuries BCE Sui led the small states of the Han River region against the State of Chu; King Wu of Chu died on campaign against it in 690 BCE. It later became a close Chu ally and sheltered King Zhao of Chu when Wu armies took Ying in 506 BCE. The tomb of Marquis Yi of Zeng, buried around 433 BCE, held 65 bronze bells, lacquerware and early writing on bamboo.
state-of-sui.e: Sui faded from the record and was absorbed by Chu, probably in the 4th century BCE. The excavation of Marquis Yi's tomb in 1978 transformed knowledge of early Chinese music and court life.

state-of-dai-di.t: A small Di kingdom in the uplands of northern Hebei, destroyed in 457 BCE when Zhao Xiangzi murdered its king at a banquet.
state-of-dai-di.o: Dai was a state of the Di peoples in the upland basins of northern Shanxi and Hebei, around modern Yuxian, on the frontier between the Chinese states and the steppe. Its date of origin is unknown; it appears in Chinese sources in the 6th and 5th centuries BCE.
state-of-dai-di.r: Dai was known for its horses and for trade between farmers and herders. Its king married the sister of Zhao Xiangzi, leader of the Zhao lineage of the State of Jin, but little else is recorded of its government.
state-of-dai-di.e: In 457 BCE Zhao Xiangzi invited the king of Dai to a feast and had him killed with a bronze ladle, then annexed Dai; his sister, the queen, is said to have killed herself with a hairpin. Dai became a base of the Zhao family, the future State of Zhao.

sovereign-council-of-asturias-and-leon.t: A Republican regional government in Asturias that declared itself sovereign when cut off from the rest of Republican Spain in 1937.
sovereign-council-of-asturias-and-leon.o: After Bilbao and Santander fell to Franco in the summer of 1937, Asturias and part of León were isolated from the Republican government in Valencia. On 24 August 1937 the Interprovincial Council at Gijón, led by the Socialist miners' leader Belarmino Tomás, declared itself sovereign.
sovereign-council-of-asturias-and-leon.r: The council took over all civil and military powers, issued its own decrees and money, and tried to organise defence of the mountains and the mining valleys with exhausted troops and few supplies. The central government saw the declaration as a step too far, but could do little.
sovereign-council-of-asturias-and-leon.e: Nationalist forces broke through in October 1937. Leaders and soldiers fled by sea, and Franco's troops entered Gijón on 21 October 1937, ending the war in the north.

sovereign-principality-of-the-united-net.t: The transitional Dutch state of 1813–1815, created as Napoleon's empire collapsed, under the returning Prince of Orange as sovereign prince.
sovereign-principality-of-the-united-net.o: After Napoleon's defeat at Leipzig, French authority in the Netherlands collapsed in November 1813. A provisional government led by Gijsbert Karel van Hogendorp invited William Frederick, son of the last stadtholder, to return. He landed at Scheveningen on 30 November and accepted the title of sovereign prince.
sovereign-principality-of-the-united-net.r: William ruled under a new constitution adopted in 1814, which gave the sovereign wide powers while keeping a States General. The new state rejected the old federal republic in favour of the unitary government created in the Batavian period. Its priority was rebuilding finances and securing allied backing at the Congress of Vienna.
sovereign-principality-of-the-united-net.e: The great powers decided to unite the northern and southern Netherlands as a barrier to France. In March 1815, during Napoleon's Hundred Days, William proclaimed himself king, creating the United Kingdom of the Netherlands.

second-republic-of-venezuela.t: The republic restored by Bolívar's Admirable Campaign of 1813, which fell within a year to the royalist llanero cavalry of José Tomás Boves.
second-republic-of-venezuela.o: In 1813 Simón Bolívar invaded Venezuela from New Granada in the Admirable Campaign, while Santiago Mariño liberated the east. Bolívar issued the Decree of War to the Death in June 1813 and entered Caracas in August, where he was acclaimed as the Liberator.
second-republic-of-venezuela.r: Bolívar ruled as dictator in the west and Mariño in the east, with little formal constitution. The war became extremely brutal. José Tomás Boves raised the llaneros, plainsmen of mixed race, against the Creole patriots, turning the conflict into a social war. In February 1814 Bolívar ordered the execution of hundreds of Spanish prisoners at La Guaira.
second-republic-of-venezuela.e: Boves defeated Bolívar at La Puerta in June 1814, and the population of Caracas fled east in the Emigration to the East. Boves was killed at Urica in December 1814, but the republic had collapsed, and Bolívar went into exile in Jamaica.

shah-armens.t: A Turkish dynasty that ruled Ahlat on Lake Van for a century, taking the title Shah-Armen, King of the Armenians.
shah-armens.o: In 1100 Sokmen al-Qutbi, a mamluk officer of the Seljuks, took Ahlat on the north-western shore of Lake Van from the Marwanids. His descendants built a principality around the lake that took its title, Shah-Armen, from the region's Armenian past.
shah-armens.r: Ahlat became a thriving city on the trade road between Iran, the Jazira and Anatolia, with a Muslim population alongside many Armenians. The longest reign was that of Sokmen II (1128-1185), who fought the Georgians and married into the Artuqid and Zengid families. The great Seljuk-era cemetery of Ahlat, with its tall carved tombstones, reflects the city's wealth in this period.
shah-armens.e: After Sokmen II died without an heir in 1185, his mamluk Begtimur ruled, followed by other slave commanders amid Ayyubid and Georgian pressure. In 1207 the Ayyubid al-Awhad took Ahlat, ending the dynasty.

sarir.t: A Christian mountain kingdom of the Avars in Dagestan, famed among Arab geographers for its golden throne and its power over the North Caucasus highlands.
sarir.o: Sarir took shape in the 6th century in the Avar lands of mountainous Dagestan, centred on Khunzakh. Arab writers say its name came from a golden throne said to have been given by a Sasanian king. Little is known of its early history beyond these later accounts.
sarir.r: Its kings ruled clans of mountain farmers and herders and were reported to control many thousands of villages. Ibn Rusta and al-Masudi describe a Christian ruler and church while most subjects followed older beliefs. Sarir was tributary to the Khazar Khaganate, allied with the Kingdom of Alania through royal marriages, and fought the Muslim rulers of Derbent.
sarir.e: After the fall of the Khazars, Islam spread into the mountains and the Christian monarchy faded in the 11th and 12th centuries. Its lands and traditions passed to the Avar Khanate, centred on the same town of Khunzakh.

state-of-han.t: The smallest of the three states carved from Jin, home of the administrator Shen Buhai and the philosopher Han Fei, and the first state conquered by Qin.
state-of-han.o: The Han lineage, ministers of the State of Jin, shared in the destruction of the Zhi clan in 453 BCE and the partition of Jin. In 403 BCE the Zhou king recognised Marquis Jing as a ruler. In 375 BCE Han conquered the State of Zheng and moved its capital to Xinzheng in Henan.
state-of-han.r: Han held a central but exposed position on the routes from Qin to the eastern plain. Under Marquis Zhao the minister Shen Buhai developed methods for controlling officials, and Han's crossbows and swords were renowned. Its prince Han Fei wrote the classic statement of Legalism. Han's attempt to exhaust Qin by having the engineer Zheng Guo build a canal backfired by enriching Qin.
state-of-han.e: Han was the first of the six states to fall: in 230 BCE the State of Qin captured King An and made his land a commandery. The name Han was later revived for the kingdom granted to a royal descendant in 206 BCE.

sheikhdom-of-sancul.t: A Swahili Muslim sheikhdom on the mainland opposite Mozambique Island, alternately ally and rival of the Portuguese.
sheikhdom-of-sancul.o: Sancul developed on the coast south of Mozambique Island as a settlement of Swahili Muslim families, many connected to Angoche and other coastal towns. By the 18th century it was governed by its own sheikhs, who held land and authority over neighbouring Makua communities.
sheikhdom-of-sancul.r: The sheikhs combined Islamic leadership with control of trade between the Makua interior and the coast. They sometimes allied with the Portuguese at Mozambique Island and sometimes resisted their demands. In the 19th century Sancul profited from the slave trade to the Comoros, Madagascar and the French islands.
sheikhdom-of-sancul.e: Sancul joined the coastal resistance to Portuguese occupation in the late 19th century. Portuguese campaigns against the Swahili sheikhdoms and the Sultanate of Angoche brought it under colonial control by 1910.

state-of-jin.t: The dominant northern power of the Spring and Autumn period, whose hegemon Duke Wen defeated Chu at Chengpu and whose break-up in 403 BCE opened the Warring States era.
state-of-jin.o: King Cheng of Zhou enfeoffed his younger brother Tang Shu Yu in the Fen River valley of southern Shanxi, among Rong and Di peoples. The early Jin rulers' cemetery at Beizhao near Tianma-Qucun has confirmed the location. In 678 BCE a junior branch of the house, from Quwo, seized power and made Jiang its capital.
state-of-jin.r: Duke Xian expanded Jin by conquering neighbours such as Western Guo and the State of Yu, and Duke Wen, the long-exiled Chong'er, became hegemon after defeating the State of Chu at Chengpu in 632 BCE. Jin dominated the north for a century and a half, but its dukes barred their own kinsmen from office and power passed to ministerial lineages commanding the state's armies.
state-of-jin.e: After the ministerial families of Han, Zhao and Wei destroyed the Zhi clan in 453 BCE, they divided Jin among themselves and were recognised as rulers by the Zhou king in 403 BCE, creating the State of Han, the State of Zhao and the State of Wei. The last Jin dukes were stripped of their remaining lands in 376 BCE.

socialist-republic-of-chile.t: A Chilean socialist republic proclaimed by military officers in June 1932, which lasted only twelve days before a counter-coup.
socialist-republic-of-chile.o: Chile was hit severely by the Great Depression, which collapsed nitrate and copper exports. On 4 June 1932 the air force commander Marmaduke Grove and other officers, with the politicians Carlos Dávila and Eugenio Matte, overthrew President Juan Esteban Montero and proclaimed the Socialist Republic of Chile.
socialist-republic-of-chile.r: A governing junta announced radical measures, including the dissolution of Congress, the distribution of land, the release of goods pawned by the poor, and plans to nationalise key industries. Divisions quickly emerged between Grove's more radical socialism and Dávila's moderate state socialism. Opposition from the army and conservative groups grew.
socialist-republic-of-chile.e: On 16 June 1932 Dávila ousted Grove and Matte, who were exiled to Easter Island. Dávila ruled until September, and after further instability, elections in October 1932 returned Arturo Alessandri to the presidency of the Republic of Chile. Grove later helped found the Socialist Party.

spanish-netherlands.t: The southern Low Countries under the Spanish Habsburgs, battleground of Europe and home of Rubens, which survived the Dutch Revolt but lost land to France.
spanish-netherlands.o: In 1555–1556 Charles V passed the Habsburg Netherlands to his son Philip II of Spain. Philip's persecution of Protestants, new bishoprics and taxes provoked the Dutch Revolt from 1566. After the Duke of Alba's harsh rule, the southern provinces made peace with Philip through the Union of Arras in 1579.
spanish-netherlands.r: The Duke of Parma reconquered Flanders and Brabant, taking Antwerp in 1585, while the north became the Dutch Republic. The Archdukes Albert and Isabella governed from 1598 to 1621 and agreed the Twelve Years' Truce. The provinces became a Counter-Reformation stronghold; Rubens worked in Antwerp. The Treaty of Münster of 1648 closed the Scheldt, hurting Antwerp's trade.
spanish-netherlands.e: Louis XIV took Artois, Lille, Cambrai and other lands between 1659 and 1678. After the War of the Spanish Succession, the Treaties of Utrecht and Rastatt in 1713–1714 gave the territory to Austria as the Austrian Netherlands.

swedish-gold-coast.t: Sweden's brief foothold in West Africa, centred on Carolusborg at Cape Coast, lost to Denmark and the Dutch within thirteen years.
swedish-gold-coast.o: The Swedish Africa Company was founded in 1649 by Louis De Geer, a Dutch-born industrialist in Swedish service. Its agent Hendrik Carloff obtained land from the local Fante rulers, and in 1653 the company built Fort Carolusborg at Cape Coast, on the coast of modern Ghana, along with smaller lodges.
swedish-gold-coast.r: The colony was a trading enterprise, exchanging European goods for gold, ivory and enslaved people. It relied on agreements with local African rulers and on Dutch and Swedish crews, and it faced constant rivalry from the Dutch West India Company and the Danes.
swedish-gold-coast.e: In 1658 Carloff, now serving Denmark, seized Carolusborg. The fort changed hands several times before the Dutch took it in 1663, ending Swedish presence in Africa. As Cape Coast Castle under the English from 1664, it became one of the main centres of the British slave trade.
