sauromatae.t: Iranian-speaking nomads between the Don and the southern Urals, ancestors of the Sarmatians, remembered by Herodotus for their armed and riding women.
sauromatae.o: Herodotus places the Sauromatae east of the Don, beyond the Royal Scythians, in the 5th century BCE, and tells the legend that they descended from Scythian men and Amazons. Archaeologists link them to the Early Sarmatian or Sauromatian culture of the lower Volga and southern Urals, which took shape around the 6th century BCE.
sauromatae.r: They lived as pastoral nomads moving between seasonal pastures, burying their dead in kurgans with weapons, bronze mirrors and stone altars. A striking feature of their graves is the number of women buried with arrows, swords and horse gear, which matches Herodotus' remark that their women rode, hunted and fought, and could not marry before killing an enemy.
sauromatae.e: From the 4th century BCE the Sauromatae merged into the larger Sarmatian confederations, including the Aorsi and Siraces, which pushed west across the Don and displaced the Scythians. Their name largely gives way to 'Sarmatians' in later Greek and Roman sources.

sweden-norway.t: Personal union of Sweden and Norway under the Bernadotte kings, created in 1814 and peacefully dissolved by Norway in 1905.
sweden-norway.o: By the Treaty of Kiel in 1814 Denmark ceded Norway to Sweden, but the Norwegians adopted a constitution at Eidsvoll and elected their own king. After a short war in the summer of 1814, the Convention of Moss allowed Norway to keep its constitution, and the Storting elected Charles XIII of Sweden as king of Norway. The Act of Union of 1815 set the terms.
sweden-norway.r: Each kingdom kept its own parliament, government, laws, army and currency, sharing only the monarch and foreign policy, which was run from Stockholm. The Bernadotte kings, starting with Charles XIV John, tried to strengthen the union, while Norwegian nationalism and parliamentary democracy grew. In 1884 Norway won parliamentary government.
sweden-norway.e: A dispute over a separate Norwegian consular service came to a head when the Storting declared on 7 June 1905 that the king had ceased to rule Norway. Norwegians voted overwhelmingly for dissolution, the Karlstad Convention settled terms peacefully, and Prince Carl of Denmark became Haakon VII of the Kingdom of Norway.

stavropol-soviet-republic.t: A short-lived Soviet republic centred on Stavropol during the first months of the Russian Civil War in 1918.
stavropol-soviet-republic.o: In early 1918 the Bolsheviks took power in Stavropol Governorate and proclaimed the Stavropol Soviet Republic as an autonomous part of the Russian SFSR. It was one of several regional Soviet republics declared in the south of Russia as the old administration collapsed.
stavropol-soviet-republic.r: Governed by a council of people's commissars, the republic covered the grain lands of Stavropol, where the peasants were largely Russian and Ukrainian settlers. It requisitioned grain and organised Red Guard units to fight the Volunteer Army and anti-Bolshevik Cossacks. Little is known of its internal administration.
stavropol-soviet-republic.e: In July 1918 it was merged into the North Caucasian Soviet Republic. The Whites took Stavropol later that year, and Soviet power returned only in 1920. The territory was later absorbed into the Soviet North Caucasus Krai.

sark.t: A tiny Channel Island fief, part of the Bailiwick of Guernsey, which kept a feudal constitution under its Seigneur until the 21st century.
sark.o: Sark was virtually empty after the 15th century due to pirates. In 1565 Elizabeth I granted it as a fief to Helier de Carteret of Jersey, on condition that he settle it with at least forty men to defend it. He divided it into forty tenements, whose holders formed its parliament, the Chief Pleas.
sark.r: Sark was governed by its Seigneur and the Chief Pleas under Norman feudal law. Cars are banned, and the island lived from farming, fishing and later tourism. Dame Sibyl Hathaway, Dame of Sark from 1927 to 1974, led the island through German occupation from 1940 to 1945.
sark.e: In 2008 Sark held its first fully democratic elections, ending its feudal constitution. It remains a self-governing part of the Bailiwick of Guernsey and a Crown Dependency.

syracuse.t: The greatest Greek city of the West, which defeated Carthage and Athens, ruled much of Sicily under its tyrants and kings, and fell to Rome in 212 BCE.
syracuse.o: Corinthian colonists led by Archias founded Syracuse in 734 or 733 BCE on the island of Ortygia, with its freshwater spring of Arethusa and two harbours. The city expanded onto the mainland and founded daughter colonies including Kamarina, controlling south-eastern Sicily.
syracuse.r: Its politics swung between aristocracy, democracy and powerful tyrants. Gelon made it the leading Greek power and with Theron of Acragas crushed Carthage at Himera in 480 BCE. A democracy defeated the Athenian expedition in 415–413 BCE. Dionysius I built the Epipolae walls and an empire over Sicily and southern Italy; Agathocles later took the title of king. Under Hieron II, Rome's ally from 263 BCE, Syracuse enjoyed peace and Archimedes worked there.
syracuse.e: After Hieron II's death Syracuse sided with Carthage. Marcus Claudius Marcellus besieged it from 214 BCE and took it in 212 BCE, when Archimedes was killed. It became the seat of the Roman governor of Sicily and remained a major city; its ancient centre is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

sultanate-of-mogadishu.t: A Muslim port city on the Benadir coast that grew rich on gold, textiles and Indian Ocean trade and minted its own coins.
sultanate-of-mogadishu.o: Mogadishu grew in the 10th century as Arab and Persian merchants settled among Somali communities on the Benadir coast. By the 13th century it had become the leading town of the region, with stone mosques such as the Mosque of Fakr ad-Din, built in 1269, and a ruling dynasty that took the title of sultan.
sultanate-of-mogadishu.r: The city controlled the gold trade from Sofala for a time and exported its own cotton cloth to Egypt and Arabia. It issued copper coins from the 13th century. Ibn Battuta, who visited in 1331, described Sultan Abu Bakr ibn Shaykh Umar, who spoke Somali (Maqdishi) and Arabic and was advised by qadis and a council of notables, and an elaborate court ceremonial.
sultanate-of-mogadishu.e: From the 16th century Mogadishu fell under the influence of the Ajuran Sultanate, and Portuguese raids disrupted its trade. With the decline of the Ajuran around 1700, power passed to the Hiraab Imamate. The old town of Hamar Weyne preserves its medieval core.

seljuk-emirate-of-damascus.t: The Damascus share of Tutush's divided realm, ruled by his son Duqaq while the First Crusade marched past.
seljuk-emirate-of-damascus.o: When Tutush I was killed in 1095, his son Duqaq took Damascus with the support of the city's garrison and the commander Tughtekin, who became his atabeg, or guardian. His brother Ridwan held Aleppo, and the two became bitter rivals.
seljuk-emirate-of-damascus.r: Duqaq's emirate covered Damascus, the Hawran and parts of the Beqaa. Its policy was dominated by the feud with Aleppo, so neither brother offered serious resistance to the Crusaders. Duqaq joined Kerbogha's relief army at Antioch in 1098, which was defeated, and fought Baldwin of Boulogne on the coast in 1100. Administration was in the hands of Tughtekin and the city's notables.
seljuk-emirate-of-damascus.e: Duqaq died in 1104. Tughtekin briefly ruled in the name of his infant son and then on his own account, founding the Burid Emirate of Damascus.

southern-ireland.t: The home-rule jurisdiction created by the Government of Ireland Act 1920 for twenty-six counties, which existed largely on paper until replaced by the Irish Free State.
southern-ireland.o: The Government of Ireland Act 1920 divided Ireland into two home-rule areas, Northern Ireland and Southern Ireland, each with its own Parliament under Westminster. Southern Ireland came into existence in May 1921, when elections were held for its House of Commons.
southern-ireland.r: Sinn Fein won 124 of the 128 seats unopposed but treated the election as one for the second Dail of the Irish Republic, so the Parliament of Southern Ireland met only twice, in June 1921 and January 1922. Only the four members for Dublin University attended the first meeting.
southern-ireland.e: Its second meeting approved the Anglo-Irish Treaty and set up the Provisional Government under Michael Collins. Southern Ireland was replaced by the Irish Free State on 6 December 1922.

strymonians.t: Slavic tribe of the lower Strymon valley that joined the sieges of Thessalonica and long resisted Byzantine control.
strymonians.o: Known mainly from the Miracles of Saint Demetrius and Byzantine chronicles, the Strymonians settled along the lower Strymon (Struma) in the early 7th century and took part in the Slavic attacks on Thessalonica around 615.
strymonians.r: They were a tribal people under local chiefs, farming the river valley and controlling routes between Thessalonica and Constantinople. In the 670s they again joined attacks on Thessalonica, and in 688 Justinian II campaigned against them and moved many Slavs to Anatolia.
strymonians.e: Byzantium gradually brought the lower Strymon under control, creating the theme of Strymon by the 9th century, while the upper valley passed to the First Bulgarian Empire. The tribe merged into the population of both.

state-of-aden.t: The former Aden Colony as a member state of the Federation of South Arabia, the scene of the Aden Emergency.
state-of-aden.o: In January 1963 the Colony of Aden entered the Federation of South Arabia as the State of Aden, keeping its own government under a chief minister, while Britain retained sovereignty and control of the military base. The merger was opposed by Aden's nationalists, who resented being joined to the hinterland rulers.
state-of-aden.r: Aden's legislature was elected on a narrow franchise. The chief minister Hassan Ali Bayoomi supported the merger; his successor Abdul Qawi Mackawee sided with the nationalists and was dismissed in 1965, after which Britain ruled directly. Strikes, bombings and assassinations by the National Liberation Front and FLOSY made Aden the centre of the emergency.
state-of-aden.e: In June 1967 armed nationalists briefly held the Crater district. British forces withdrew in November 1967 and Aden became the capital of South Yemen.

southern-song.t: The Song dynasty's southern phase, ruled from Hangzhou, when China led the world in commerce, technology and learning before falling to the Mongols.
southern-song.o: When the Jurchen of the Jin dynasty (1115-1234) captured Kaifeng in 1127, Zhao Gou, a son of Emperor Huizong, was enthroned as Emperor Gaozong. Pursued south, he eventually fixed his court at Lin'an (Hangzhou). The Treaty of Shaoxing in 1141 recognised the Huai river as the frontier, after the execution of the general Yue Fei.
southern-song.r: Cut off from the north, the Song Dynasty flourished in the south. Rice agriculture, porcelain, silk and printing expanded; paper money circulated widely; and Quanzhou became one of the world's great ports. A permanent navy guarded the Yangtze and coast. Zhu Xi's Neo-Confucianism became orthodoxy, and Hangzhou was perhaps the world's largest city.
southern-song.e: Song joined the Mongols to destroy Jin in 1234, then faced the Mongol Empire alone. After the long siege of Xiangyang ended in 1273, Lin'an surrendered in 1276. At the naval Battle of Yamen in 1279 the minister Lu Xiufu leapt into the sea with the boy emperor, and the Yuan Dynasty ruled all China.

south-yemen.t: The only Marxist state in the Arab world, ruled from Aden by the Yemeni Socialist Party until unification with the North in 1990.
south-yemen.o: On 30 November 1967, after Britain withdrew from the Federation of South Arabia, the National Liberation Front proclaimed the People's Republic of South Yemen with Qahtan al-Shaabi as president. The sultanates and sheikhdoms of the former Aden Protectorate were abolished.
south-yemen.r: A leftward shift in 1969 removed al-Shaabi, and in 1970 the country became the People's Democratic Republic of Yemen. The ruling party, from 1978 the Yemeni Socialist Party, nationalised land and industry, expanded education and women's rights and allied with the Soviet Union, which used Aden as a base. It supported the Dhofar rebellion in Oman. Aden's port declined after the Suez Canal closed in 1967.
south-yemen.e: Party rivalries erupted in a brief civil war in Aden in January 1986 that killed thousands. Weakened by the end of Soviet aid, South Yemen united with the Yemen Arab Republic on 22 May 1990 to form the Republic of Yemen.

second-hungarian-republic.t: Hungary's brief post-war multi-party republic, which suffered the worst hyperinflation in history and was dismantled step by step by the communists.
second-hungarian-republic.o: After the Soviet army drove German forces from Hungary in 1945, free elections in November 1945 gave the Independent Smallholders' Party an absolute majority. The parliament abolished the monarchy of the Kingdom of Hungary (1920-1946) and proclaimed a republic on 1 February 1946, with the Smallholder Zoltán Tildy as president and Ferenc Nagy as prime minister.
second-hungarian-republic.r: Under Soviet occupation the communists of Mátyás Rákosi controlled the interior ministry and police and broke up rival parties by 'salami tactics'. The pengő collapsed in the worst hyperinflation ever recorded until the forint was introduced in August 1946. Land reform divided the great estates. Smallholder leader Béla Kovács was arrested by Soviet forces in 1947 and Nagy forced into exile.
second-hungarian-republic.e: Manipulated elections in 1947, the merger of the Social Democrats into a communist party in 1948 and the arrest of Cardinal Mindszenty ended pluralism. A Soviet-style constitution created the Hungarian People's Republic on 20 August 1949.

swellendam-republic.t: A short-lived republic declared by Cape frontier burghers who expelled the Dutch East India Company's officials in 1795.
swellendam-republic.o: By 1795 burghers in the Swellendam district east of Cape Town resented the Dutch East India Company's trade restrictions, taxes and its failure to defend them on the frontier. In June 1795, following the example of Graaff-Reinet, they expelled the landdrost and proclaimed themselves a free republic, choosing Hermanus Steyn as president of their assembly.
swellendam-republic.r: Inspired partly by the ideas of the French Revolution, the burghers set up an assembly of national representatives to run local affairs. They demanded free trade, lower taxes and a free hand in dealings with the Khoikhoi and the Xhosa.
swellendam-republic.e: British forces occupied the Cape in September 1795 after the Battle of Muizenberg, and the Swellendam burghers accepted British authority later that year, ending the republic within months.

shaib-sheikhdom.t: One of the smallest states of the British Aden Protectorate, a tribal sheikhdom in the highlands near Dhala.
shaib-sheikhdom.o: The Shaib tribe held a small mountain territory near the Emirate of Dhala, with its seat at Al Awabil. It emerged as a separate sheikhdom around 1800, when the Qasimid State no longer controlled the region. Its early history is almost unknown.
shaib-sheikhdom.r: The sheikhs governed a few thousand tribespeople who farmed terraced valleys. The sheikhdom was brought into the Aden Protectorate by treaty with Britain and joined the Federation of South Arabia in the 1960s.
shaib-sheikhdom.e: After the National Liberation Front took power in 1967, the sheikhdom was abolished and incorporated into South Yemen.

selge.t: Selge, a powerful Pisidian mountain city in the Taurus, which claimed Spartan origins and fielded armies of thousands.
selge.o: Selge was founded in the high Taurus north of Pamphylia, above the Eurymedon gorge. Its citizens claimed descent from Spartans and from the seer Calchas, but the city grew from a Pisidian community that became increasingly Greek from the 5th century BCE.
selge.r: Selge was a self-governing city controlling fertile upland valleys that produced olives, wine and storax resin used in perfume. Polybius says it could field 20,000 men, and in 218 BCE it resisted a siege by the Seleucid general Achaeus.
selge.e: Selge kept its independence until Rome organised the region. In 25 BCE it became part of the province of Galatia and lived on as a Roman provincial town.

seventeenth-dynasty-of-egypt.t: The Theban kings who began the war that drove the Hyksos from Egypt and paved the way for the New Kingdom.
seventeenth-dynasty-of-egypt.o: Around 1580 BCE a new line of kings took power at Thebes, following the Sixteenth Dynasty of Egypt. At first they acknowledged the overlordship of the Hyksos Fifteenth Dynasty of Egypt in the north and the power of Kerma in the south, and ruled Upper Egypt from Elephantine to Abydos.
seventeenth-dynasty-of-egypt.r: The Theban court was modest, its kings buried in small pyramids at Dra Abu el-Naga, but it built up a strong army. Seqenenre Tao began open war with the Hyksos king Apepi, and his mummy shows fatal head wounds from axes. His successor Kamose campaigned north to the walls of Avaris, and his stelae at Karnak record an intercepted letter from Apepi to the ruler of Kush.
seventeenth-dynasty-of-egypt.e: Kamose's brother Ahmose I completed the war, taking Avaris around 1550 BCE and reuniting Egypt. His reign is counted as the start of the Eighteenth Dynasty and the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom.

simyra.t: Simyra, a port on the Syrian coast that served as Egypt's northern base and later the capital of Amurru, until Assyria made it a province.
simyra.o: Sumur, probably Tell Kazel near the Lebanese border, controlled the Akkar plain and the gap leading inland to the Orontes. In the 15th century BCE Thutmose III of the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom made it a garrison and administrative centre for his Syrian conquests.
simyra.r: The Amarna letters show an Egyptian commissioner residing there. Abdi-Ashirta and his son Aziru seized it, and it became the capital of the Kingdom of Amurru. In the Iron Age it was a Phoenician town whose people, the Zemarites, are listed in Genesis.
simyra.e: Simyra was occupied by Tiglath-Pileser III of the Assyrian Empire in 738 BCE and became the centre of an Assyrian province. Later overshadowed by Arwad, it shrank to a minor town.

state-of-chen.t: A Zhou state on the Huai plain whose rulers claimed descent from the sage-king Shun, a frequent victim of Chu whose exiled branch later seized the throne of Qi.
state-of-chen.o: King Wu of Zhou enfeoffed Gui Man, Duke Hu of Chen, a descendant of the legendary Emperor Shun, at Wanqiu (modern Huaiyang, Henan), and gave him his eldest daughter in marriage. Chen thus combined ancient lineage with close ties to the royal house.
state-of-chen.r: Chen sat on the open plain between the northern states and the State of Chu, and switched allegiance repeatedly. Its court was notorious for intrigue: Duke Ling was killed in 599 BCE by Xia Zhengshu, prompting a Chu intervention. In 672 BCE Prince Wan of Chen fled to the State of Qi, where his descendants, the Tian clan, rose to power. Confucius was famously stranded between Chen and Cai.
state-of-chen.e: Chu occupied Chen twice before King Hui of Chu annexed it for good in 479 BCE. Its capital became an important Chu city, and in 278 BCE served as the Chu capital after Ying fell to Qin. The Tian lineage descended from Chen ruled Qi until 221 BCE.

senones-400.t: Gaulish people of the Adriatic coast of the Marche, credited with the sack of Rome in 390 BCE and destroyed by Rome in 283 BCE.
senones-400.o: The Senones were, according to Polybius and Livy, the last of the Celtic peoples to cross into Italy, around 400 BCE. They settled on the Adriatic coast between the Utente and Esino rivers, land later called the Ager Gallicus, displacing Umbrians and Etruscan settlers.
senones-400.r: They lived in villages and buried their warriors with weapons and imported Etruscan and Greek goods, as at Montefortino and Filottrano. Roman tradition said Senones led by Brennus defeated Rome at the Allia and sacked the city in 390 BCE. They raided central Italy and served as mercenaries, including for Dionysius I.
senones-400.e: The Senones fought alongside the Samnites at Sentinum in 295 BCE. After they defeated a Roman army at Arretium in 284 BCE, Publius Cornelius Dolabella expelled or destroyed them in 283 BCE, and the colony of Sena Gallica (Senigallia) was founded on their land.

second-athenian-league.t: Alliance of Aegean states formed by Athens in 378 BCE to resist Sparta, with promises not to repeat the abuses of the 5th-century empire.
second-athenian-league.o: Spartan high-handedness after the King's Peace of 386 BCE, and a raid on Attica by the Spartan Sphodrias, pushed Athens to found a new alliance in 378-377 BCE. The surviving decree of Aristoteles invites Greeks and barbarians to join 'so that the Spartans may allow the Greeks to be free', listing members such as Chios, Thebes and Byzantium.
second-athenian-league.r: Members kept their autonomy and constitutions, and Athens renounced garrisons, governors, tribute and Athenian settlement on allied land. Allies sat in a council (synedrion) at Athens that voted alongside the Athenian assembly and paid 'contributions' rather than tribute. At its height some seventy states joined. Chabrias' naval victory off Naxos in 376 BCE restored Athenian sea power.
second-athenian-league.e: Athens gradually broke its promises, planting settlers on Samos. In the Social War of 357-355 BCE Chios, Rhodes, Cos and Byzantium, encouraged by Mausolus of Caria, left the league. Reduced to a rump, it ended after Philip II's victory at Chaeronea in 338 BCE and the creation of the League of Corinth.

saltukids.t: One of the first Turkish principalities in eastern Anatolia, ruling Erzurum and fighting Georgia for over a century.
saltukids.o: Tradition holds that the Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan granted the region of Erzurum to the commander Saltuk after the victory at Manzikert in 1071. His descendants established a hereditary emirate there, among the earliest Turkish states in Anatolia.
saltukids.r: The Saltukids held Erzurum, Tercan, Ispir and Kars at times, on the frontier with the Kingdom of Georgia, which defeated them several times; Izz al-Din Saltuk II was captured by the Georgians in the 1150s and ransomed. Erzurum prospered from the trade route between Iran and the Black Sea. Surviving monuments include the tomb tower of Emir Saltuk and the Tepsi Minaret in Erzurum.
saltukids.e: In 1202 the Rum Seljuk sultan Suleymanshah II, campaigning against Georgia, annexed Erzurum and gave it to his brother Tughrilshah, ending the dynasty.

smolyani.t: Slavic tribe of the Rhodope Mountains and Mesta valley, known from Byzantine sources until it passed under Bulgarian rule in the 9th century.
smolyani.o: The Smolyani were among the Slavic groups who settled the Balkans in the late 6th and 7th centuries, taking the Rhodopes and the middle Mesta (Nestos) in modern Bulgaria and Greece. They are named among the tribes that besieged Thessalonica in the 670s.
smolyani.r: Known only from brief Byzantine mentions, they were a tribal people under local chiefs, nominally subject to Byzantium, farming and herding in the mountain valleys. The modern town of Smolyan preserves their name.
smolyani.e: In 837 the Smolyani rose against Byzantine rule, and Khan Presian of the First Bulgarian Empire used the revolt to take their lands, which were absorbed into Bulgaria.

siris.t: Short-lived Ionian Greek city on the Gulf of Taranto, proverbial for wealth, destroyed by its Achaean neighbours in the 6th century BCE.
siris.o: Ionian Greeks from Colophon in Asia Minor, fleeing Lydian attacks, founded Siris around 680 BCE near the mouth of the Siris (Sinni) river, apparently taking over an existing native settlement. The poet Archilochus praised its land as fair and lovely.
siris.r: Little is known of its government. Siris was famous for its fertile land and luxury, like its neighbour Sybaris, and became a rival to the Achaean cities of Metapontum, Sybaris and Croton. Some scholars link the hill of Policoro with its main settlement. Herodotus records that Athens later claimed a right to the site.
siris.e: Around 530 BCE an alliance of Metapontum, Sybaris and Croton captured Siris and destroyed it, reportedly killing suppliants at the altar of Athena. In 433 BCE Taras and Thurii founded Heraclea on or near its territory.

sultanate-of-nejd.t: Ibn Saud's state after the conquest of Ha'il, which fixed its northern borders and launched the conquest of the Hejaz.
sultanate-of-nejd.o: In 1921, after taking Ha'il and ending the Emirate of Jabal Shammar, Abd al-Aziz ibn Saud adopted the title Sultan of Nejd and its Dependencies, replacing the Emirate of Nejd and Hasa. Britain, his ally under the Treaty of Darin, recognised the new title.
sultanate-of-nejd.r: The sultanate covered central and eastern Arabia and, from 1920, highland Asir. Its frontiers with the new British mandates were set at the Uqair conference of 1922, which drew the borders with the Sheikhdom of Kuwait and the Kingdom of Iraq and created two neutral zones. The Ikhwan raided Transjordan, Iraq and Kuwait, causing clashes with British forces. In 1924 they attacked the Kingdom of Hejaz.
sultanate-of-nejd.e: After Mecca and then Jeddah fell, Ibn Saud was proclaimed King of the Hejaz in January 1926, joining his two realms as the Kingdom of Hejaz and Nejd.

septinsular-republic.t: Republic of the Seven Islands under Russian and Ottoman protection, the first self-governing Greek state of modern times.
septinsular-republic.o: In 1798-1799 a joint Russian-Ottoman expedition under Admiral Fyodor Ushakov drove the French from the Ionian Islands. The Treaty of Constantinople in 1800 created the Septinsular Republic of Corfu, Paxos, Lefkada, Ithaca, Cephalonia, Zakynthos and Kythira, under Ottoman suzerainty and Russian protection.
septinsular-republic.r: The republic was governed by a senate in Corfu dominated by the island nobility, under a series of constitutions; that of 1803 widened participation. Count Spyridon Theotokis presided over the senate, and the young Ioannis Kapodistrias, later the first governor of Greece, served as secretary of state. Greek became an official language alongside Italian.
septinsular-republic.e: At Tilsit in 1807 Russia ceded the islands to Napoleon, and they returned to French rule as the French Ionian Islands. The republic's experience of self-rule fed the ideas of the Greek national movement.

stellaland.t: A Boer mini-republic around Vryburg, created by mercenaries paid in land, whose fate was decided by imperial rivalry.
stellaland.o: In 1882 the Tlhaping chief Mankurwane and the Korana chief David Massouw fought over land west of the Transvaal, both recruiting white mercenaries. Those who served Massouw received farms and proclaimed the Republic of Stellaland, named after a comet, with Gerrit Jacobus van Niekerk as administrator and Vryburg as capital.
stellaland.r: The republic had a Volksraad, issued postage stamps and joined with neighbouring Goshen in 1883 as the United States of Stellaland. Its settlers farmed cattle and sought union with the South African Republic, which would have cut Britain's road north to the interior.
stellaland.e: Cecil Rhodes and the Cape government pressed for British intervention. Sir Charles Warren's expedition arrived in 1885, and Stellaland was absorbed into British Bechuanaland; Vryburg became its capital.

sultanate-of-rafai.t: A Zande sultanate on the Mbomou River whose rulers traded ivory and captives before falling under French rule.
sultanate-of-rafai.o: The Rafai state was one of several Zande-ruled sultanates that formed along the Mbomou River in the 19th century. It took its name from its ruler Rafai, whose followers controlled the area around the town that still bears the name.
sultanate-of-rafai.r: Little is recorded in detail. Like its neighbours, the sultanate depended on armed retainers, tribute and the sale of ivory and captives to traders coming from the Nile basin, which supplied firearms.
sultanate-of-rafai.e: In the 1890s it dealt with officers of the Congo Free State and then, after the 1894 boundary agreement, with France. Its independent power ended when it was absorbed into Ubangi-Shari in the early 20th century.

simsir.t: A short-lived Muslim principality of the Chechens on the North Caucasus plain, known almost only from the chronicles of Timur's campaign of 1395.
simsir.o: After the Mongol conquest, Chechen communities on the plains north of the mountains came under the Golden Horde. In the 14th century a principality called Simsir formed there, apparently around the middle Sunzha and Argun rivers. Its origins are not recorded.
simsir.r: Persian chroniclers of Timur, notably Sharaf al-Din Yazdi, mention its ruler Ghayur Khan and describe Simsir as a Muslim land, one of the first among the Chechens. It paid tribute to the Golden Horde and sided with Tokhtamysh in his war against Timur.
simsir.e: In 1395 Timur's army devastated Simsir during its campaign against Tokhtamysh, and the principality disappears from the record. Its people withdrew to the mountains, and the plain was resettled only later.

state-of-maranhao.t: A separate Portuguese colony covering the Amazon and the north coast of Brazil, governed directly from Lisbon rather than from Salvador.
state-of-maranhao.o: After expelling the French of Equinoctial France in 1615 and founding Belém in 1616, Portugal created the State of Maranhão in 1621, separate from the State of Brazil. Its capital was São Luís, and it included Grão-Pará, Ceará and the Amazon basin, which were easier to reach by sea from Lisbon than from Salvador.
state-of-maranhao.r: The colony depended on indigenous labour to collect forest products such as cacao, cloves and sarsaparilla. Pedro Teixeira's expedition up the Amazon in 1637 to 1639 extended Portuguese claims. The Dutch held São Luís from 1641 to 1644. The Jesuit António Vieira campaigned against the enslavement of indigenous people. Settlers resented Jesuit control and a trading company's monopoly, which led to the Beckman Revolt in 1684.
state-of-maranhao.e: In 1751 the Marquis of Pombal reorganised the colony as the State of Grão-Pará and Maranhão, with its capital moved to Belém and his brother Francisco Xavier de Mendonça Furtado as governor.

sultanate-of-anjouan.t: The leading Comorian sultanate, known to English sailors as Johanna, a provisioning stop on the route to India until French rule.
sultanate-of-anjouan.o: Shirazi-descended families established a sultanate on Anjouan (Ndzuwani) around 1500, with an early capital at Domoni. The ruling house later moved to Mutsamudu on the north-west coast, which grew into a fortified stone town with a citadel overlooking its harbour.
sultanate-of-anjouan.r: The sultan governed with a council of the leading Arab and Shirazi lineages, while much of the rural population lived in dependence or slavery. Anjouan prospered by supplying East India Company and other European ships with water, cattle and fruit, and English became widely understood at court. The sultans claimed overlordship of Mayotte and Moheli and fought repeatedly to enforce it.
sultanate-of-anjouan.e: Civil wars and Malagasy raids weakened the island in the 19th century. Sultan Abdallah III accepted a French protectorate in 1886, and France annexed the island outright in 1912. Anjouan became part of the independent Comoros in 1975, though it attempted secession in 1997.

salassi.t: Alpine people of the Aosta valley who controlled the Great and Little St Bernard passes and their gold, and resisted Rome until 25 BCE.
salassi.o: The Salassi lived in the Aosta valley and around Eporedia (Ivrea), at the foot of the passes over the western Alps. Ancient writers called them Celts, though they probably mixed with earlier Ligurian peoples. They appear in Roman history in the 2nd century BCE.
salassi.r: The Salassi controlled the routes over the Alpine passes, charging tolls on travellers and armies. They worked gold deposits in the Dora Baltea valley by washing, and their disputes with Roman contractors over water rights, recorded by Strabo, led to conflict. They lived in villages and fortified places and had no known central capital.
salassi.e: Appius Claudius Pulcher fought them in 143 BCE, and Rome founded Eporedia in 100 BCE. In 25 BCE Aulus Terentius Varro Murena conquered them for Augustus, selling some 36,000 into slavery, and founded Augusta Praetoria, modern Aosta, on their land.

state-of-xi.t: A small Ji-clan state on the Huai whose fall around 680 BCE is tied to the story of Lady Xi, the silent queen taken by King Wen of Chu.
state-of-xi.o: Xi was a minor Zhou state ruled by the Ji clan, located near modern Xixian in southern Henan, on the northern edge of the Huai River plain. It lay close to the State of Cai and within reach of the expanding State of Chu.
state-of-xi.r: Little is recorded about its government. Xi appears in the Zuo zhuan chiefly in a story of feuding: the Marquis of Xi, angered that the Marquis of Cai had insulted his wife, Xi Gui, invited Chu to attack Cai, setting off a chain of events that drew Chu into the region.
state-of-xi.e: King Wen of Chu destroyed Xi around 680 BCE and took Xi Gui as his wife; she bore the future King Cheng but, by tradition, refused to speak to her new husband. Xi became a Chu county, an early example of Chu's administrative districts.

senior-juz.t: The southern division of the Kazakh people in Zhetysu, which suffered Dzungar and Kokandi rule before passing to Russia.
senior-juz.o: The Kazakhs had long been grouped into three juz, or hordes, and after the death of Tauke Khan around 1718 the Kazakh Khanate lost its unity, with each juz under its own khans. The Senior Juz occupied the south-east, from the Syr Darya to the Ili valley in Zhetysu.
senior-juz.r: Its tribes, such as the Dulat, Uysun and Jalayir, were nomadic herders closely tied to the oasis cities of Tashkent and Turkistan. They were hit hardest by the Dzungar invasions of the 1720s and partly ruled by the Dzungars until the 1750s. The judge Tole Bi, one of three famous Kazakh biys, was a leading figure.
senior-juz.e: In the early 19th century much of the Senior Juz fell under the Khanate of Kokand and the Tashkent Hakimate. From the 1820s its northern clans accepted Russian protection, and by 1848 Russia had abolished the khanship, incorporating it into the Russian Empire.

soviet-union.t: The world's first communist state and a Cold War superpower, a union of Soviet republics that stretched from the Baltic to the Pacific.
soviet-union.o: After winning the Civil War, the Bolsheviks formalised relations between the Soviet republics. In December 1922 the Russian SFSR, the Ukrainian SSR, the Byelorussian SSR and the Transcaucasian republic signed the treaty creating the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, with Moscow as capital and Vladimir Lenin as head of government.
soviet-union.r: The Communist Party ruled through a centralised planned economy. Under Joseph Stalin, five-year plans industrialised the country while collectivisation brought famine and the Great Terror killed hundreds of thousands. The Soviet Union lost about 27 million people defeating Nazi Germany, then dominated Eastern Europe, built nuclear weapons and launched Sputnik in 1957 and Yuri Gagarin in 1961.
soviet-union.e: After decades of stagnation, Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms of glasnost and perestroika loosened control, and the republics demanded independence. After a failed hardline coup in August 1991, the leaders of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus signed the Belovezha Accords, and the Soviet Union was dissolved on 26 December 1991.

south-african-republic.t: The Boer republic of the Transvaal, transformed by the Witwatersrand gold rush and destroyed by Britain in the Second Boer War.
south-african-republic.o: In the Sand River Convention of 1852 Britain recognised the independence of the Boers north of the Vaal. The separate communities, including the Potchefstroom Republic, Lydenburg and Zoutpansberg, gradually united, adopting a constitution in 1858 under President Marthinus Wessel Pretorius and making Pretoria the capital in 1860.
south-african-republic.r: Only white men could be citizens, and the constitution declared no equality between black and white. Britain annexed the bankrupt republic in 1877, but the Boers rebelled and won at Majuba in 1881. Under Paul Kruger, president from 1883, gold discovered on the Witwatersrand in 1886 made it the richest state in Africa, attracting foreign uitlanders whom Kruger kept from the vote.
south-african-republic.e: The Jameson Raid of 1895-1896 deepened conflict with Britain, which went to war in 1899. Pretoria fell in 1900, and after guerrilla war the Treaty of Vereeniging in 1902 made the republic the Transvaal Colony.

sultanate-of-itsandra.t: One of the rival sultanates of Grande Comore, whose rulers long competed with Bambao for the island's paramount title.
sultanate-of-itsandra.o: Grande Comore (Ngazidja) was divided among several Shirazi-descended lineages from around the 15th century, each ruling a district from a walled stone town. Itsandra, on the west coast north of Moroni, became one of the most powerful of these by about 1500.
sultanate-of-itsandra.r: The sultan ruled with the elders of the leading lineages under a matrilineal succession system, and Islam shaped law and town life. The island's sultans contested the title of sultan tibe, a paramount position over the others, and Itsandra and the Sultanate of Bambao were the main rivals. Wealth came from trade with the Swahili coast and Madagascar.
sultanate-of-itsandra.e: Prolonged wars between the sultanates weakened Itsandra in the 19th century. In 1886 Said Ali of Bambao accepted a French protectorate over the whole island, ending Itsandra's independence. Grande Comore later became part of the Comoros.

state-of-bahrain.t: Independent Bahrain since 1971, a Gulf financial centre ruled by the Al Khalifa and a kingdom since 2002.
state-of-bahrain.o: After a United Nations mission found that Bahrainis wanted independence rather than union with Iran, Britain ended its protection of the Sheikhdom of Bahrain, and the State of Bahrain became independent on 15 August 1971 under Isa bin Salman Al Khalifa.
state-of-bahrain.r: An elected parliament created by the constitution of 1973 was dissolved in 1975. With modest oil reserves, Bahrain built an offshore banking sector, aluminium smelting and a causeway to Saudi Arabia, opened in 1986, and hosts the US Fifth Fleet. Tension between the Sunni ruling family and the Shi'a majority produced unrest in the 1990s. Hamad bin Isa, ruler from 1999, introduced a National Action Charter and proclaimed a kingdom in 2002.
state-of-bahrain.e: In 2011 mass protests at the Pearl Roundabout were suppressed with the help of Saudi and Emirati forces. Bahrain remains a constitutional monarchy with strong royal power; it normalised relations with Israel in 2020.

state-of-wey.t: A Ji-clan state planted in the old Shang heartland that outlived every other Zhou state, surviving as a single city until 209 BCE.
state-of-wey.o: After the rebellion of the Three Guards, the Duke of Zhou gave the former Shang capital region around Zhaoge in northern Henan to Kang Shu Feng, a younger brother of King Wu, to watch over the conquered Shang population. Wey is spelt so in English to distinguish it from the State of Wei.
state-of-wey.r: Wey was a large and cultured state early in the Spring and Autumn period, and its folk songs make up a large part of the Book of Songs. In 660 BCE the Di overran it after Duke Yi, notorious for giving his cranes official carriages, was killed. Rebuilt with help from the State of Qi, it moved to Chuqiu and then Diqiu (modern Puyang). Confucius spent years there, and the reformer Shang Yang was a Wey nobleman.
state-of-wey.e: Wey shrank to the area around Puyang, a vassal first of the State of Wei and then of the State of Qin, which spared it even after unification. In 209 BCE the Second Emperor of Qin deposed Lord Jue and made him a commoner, ending the last Zhou state.

state-of-song.t: The state where the descendants of the Shang kings kept their ancestral rites under Zhou rule, home of Zhuangzi and the scene of China's first disarmament conference.
state-of-song.o: After the failed rebellion of the Shang prince Wu Geng, the Duke of Zhou installed Weizi Qi, an elder brother of the last Shang king, at Shangqiu in eastern Henan, so that the Shang royal sacrifices would continue. Song was ranked as a duchy, the highest grade of Zhou state.
state-of-song.r: Song preserved Shang customs, and other states mocked its people as slow-witted in stories like the farmer waiting by a tree stump. Duke Xiang of Song sought the hegemony but lost to the State of Chu at the Battle of Hong in 638 BCE after refusing to attack the enemy mid-crossing. In 546 BCE the Song minister Xiang Xu hosted a peace conference of fourteen states. The philosopher Zhuangzi was a native of Song.
state-of-song.e: King Yan of Song, who took the royal title, conquered the State of Teng and fought his neighbours until the State of Qi, with Wei and Chu, destroyed Song in 286 BCE and divided its lands. Song was later used as a dynastic name, most notably by the Song Dynasty.

swaziland-protectorate.t: The British protectorate over the Swazi kingdom, during which King Sobhuza II fought to recover land lost to concessions.
swaziland-protectorate.o: The South African Republic had administered Swaziland from 1894. After the Second Boer War, Britain took over in 1903 and placed it under the High Commissioner for South Africa, with Mbabane as the administrative centre.
swaziland-protectorate.r: In 1907 a partition of land left only about a third for Swazi use, the rest going to concession holders and settlers. The queen regent Labotsibeni led opposition until Sobhuza II came of age in 1921; he petitioned the Privy Council and later bought back land through a national fund. Mining of asbestos and iron and forestry grew after the Second World War.
swaziland-protectorate.e: Swaziland became independent on 6 September 1968 with Sobhuza II as king, part of the continuity of the Swazi Kingdom. He abolished the constitution in 1973, and the country was renamed Eswatini in 2018.

subalpine-republic.t: A French-controlled republic in Piedmont between Napoleon's victory at Marengo and the region's annexation to France in 1802.
subalpine-republic.o: Napoleon's victory at Marengo in June 1800 restored French control over Piedmont, which had been lost in 1799. The French set up a new government for the former mainland territories of the Kingdom of Sardinia, which became known as the Subalpine Republic.
subalpine-republic.r: The republic was administered by a commission under French supervision, with General Jourdan as administrator general from 1801. It introduced French administrative divisions and laws, abolished remaining feudal rights and prepared Piedmont for annexation. Piedmontese opinion was divided between those favouring France and those hoping for an Italian republic.
subalpine-republic.e: In September 1802 Piedmont was formally annexed to France and divided into French departments. It returned to the Kingdom of Sardinia in 1814.

state-of-teng.t: A tiny Ji-clan state in Shandong whose ruler asked Mencius how a small state could survive among giants, a dialogue preserved in the Confucian classics.
state-of-teng.o: King Wu of Zhou enfeoffed his younger brother Cuo Shu Xiu at Teng, near modern Tengzhou in south-western Shandong, as part of the network of royal kinsmen planted across the eastern plain after the conquest of the Shang.
state-of-teng.r: Teng was among the smallest Zhou states, ranked as a marquisate but forced to follow larger neighbours such as the State of Lu, the State of Qi and the State of Song. In the late 4th century BCE Duke Wen of Teng consulted Mencius on mourning rites and the well-field system of land allotment; their conversations form a chapter of the Mencius.
state-of-teng.e: Teng was conquered by the State of Song under its last king, Yan, around 296 BCE, and its lands later passed to Qi and Chu. Its memory survives chiefly through Mencius, and in the name of the city of Tengzhou.

shamkhalate-of-tarki.t: The Kumyk state on Dagestan's Caspian coast, heir of the old shamkhals, which Peter the Great visited in 1722 and Russia absorbed in 1867.
shamkhalate-of-tarki.o: Around 1642, as the Kazikumukh Shamkhalate split, the shamkhals moved their seat from the Lak mountains to Tarki, on the Caspian plain near modern Makhachkala. The new state was centred on the Kumyk people and controlled the coastal road between Derbent and the Terek.
shamkhalate-of-tarki.r: The shamkhals ruled Kumyk nobles and villages and claimed authority over much of northern Dagestan, receiving subsidies from the Safavid Empire and courting Russia and the Ottomans in turn. The plain provided grain, livestock and trade routes. During his Persian campaign Peter the Great was received at Tarki in 1722 by Shamkhal Adil-Girey, who later rebelled and died in Russian exile.
shamkhalate-of-tarki.e: The shamkhals accepted Russian protection in 1806 and held Russian military rank; Mehdi II was a loyal ally against Shamil. In 1867 the Russian Empire abolished the shamkhalate and incorporated it into the Dagestan Oblast.

state-of-lu.t: The Shandong state founded for the Duke of Zhou's line, guardian of Zhou ritual, birthplace of Confucius and subject of the Spring and Autumn Annals.
state-of-lu.o: After the Zhou conquest the Duke of Zhou was granted Lu but stayed at court as regent, sending his son Boqin to govern it. Its capital Qufu, in south-western Shandong, was built on land associated with the earlier Shang ally Yan, and Lu was charged with keeping order among the eastern peoples.
state-of-lu.r: As the house of the Duke of Zhou, Lu was allowed to perform royal rites and kept the most complete Zhou ritual and musical traditions. Its court chronicle, the Spring and Autumn Annals, covering 722 to 481 BCE, gave its name to the era. Power slipped from the dukes to three ministerial families, the Jisun, Mengsun and Shusun. Confucius, born in Lu in 551 BCE, served briefly in its government.
state-of-lu.e: Lu declined into a minor state during the Warring States period and was annexed by the State of Chu under King Kaolie in 256 BCE. Qufu remained the centre of the cult of Confucius, and the Temple and Cemetery of Confucius there are now a World Heritage Site.

second-hellenic-republic.t: The Greek republic of 1924-1935, born from the Asia Minor disaster and marked by coups, refugee resettlement and the last Venizelos government.
second-hellenic-republic.o: Greece's defeat in Asia Minor in 1922 discredited the monarchy. A military revolution forced Constantine I to abdicate, and in March 1924 the assembly proclaimed a republic, confirmed by a referendum in April. The Kingdom of Greece was thus replaced, with Admiral Pavlos Kountouriotis as first president.
second-hellenic-republic.r: The republic had to absorb more than a million refugees from Anatolia after the population exchange with Turkey, resettling many in Macedonia. Politics were unstable: General Theodoros Pangalos ruled as dictator in 1925-1926. The Venizelos government of 1928-1932 brought stability, a peace treaty with Turkey and public works, but the Great Depression ended it.
second-hellenic-republic.e: Royalists won the 1933 elections, and a failed Venizelist coup in March 1935 strengthened them. In October 1935 General Georgios Kondylis seized power, and a rigged plebiscite restored the monarchy, bringing back George II.

sajid-emirate.t: An Abbasid governorship turned hereditary emirate in Azerbaijan whose emir Yusuf dominated Armenia and executed its king Smbat I.
sajid-emirate.o: The Sajids were descended from a military family from Ushrusana in Central Asia, in the service of the caliphs. In 889 Muhammad ibn Abi'l-Saj was appointed governor of Azerbaijan and ruled it almost independently from Maragha and later Ardabil, founding a hereditary emirate under the Abbasid Caliphate.
sajid-emirate.r: The emirs controlled north-western Iran and claimed authority over Armenia and Albania as Abbasid governors, collecting tribute and backing rival Armenian princes. Yusuf ibn Abi'l-Saj invaded Armenia, captured Smbat I of Bagratid Armenia and had him executed in 914, while crowning Gagik Artsruni of the Kingdom of Vaspurakan as a rival king.
sajid-emirate.e: Yusuf was killed in 928 fighting the Qarmatians in Iraq, and the emirate collapsed in 929 amid struggles among his commanders. The Sallarid Emirate and other local dynasties took over Azerbaijan.

shaddadid-emirate.t: A Kurdish dynasty that ruled Ganja and Arran in the 10th and 11th centuries, a meeting point of Muslim, Armenian and Georgian worlds.
shaddadid-emirate.o: The Shaddadids were a Kurdish family who exploited the decline of the Sallarid Emirate. In 951 Muhammad ibn Shaddad seized Dvin, and his descendants established their seat at Ganja in Arran, taking over the region between the Kura and the Araxes.
shaddadid-emirate.r: The emirs ruled a mixed population of Muslims and Christians and fought and allied in turn with the Armenian kings of Ani, the Georgians and the Byzantines. Abu'l-Aswar Shavur, who ruled from 1049, was a forceful soldier and patron. Ganja prospered as a market city on routes linking the Caspian, Iran and the Caucasus.
shaddadid-emirate.e: The Seljuk Empire took control of Arran, and in 1075 the Seljuk sultan Malik Shah deposed the Ganja line. A branch survived as the Shaddadids of Ani, governing the former Armenian capital for the Seljuks.

sakala.t: Estonian county around Viljandi, homeland of the elder Lembitu, who led the most determined resistance to the Livonian crusade.
sakala.o: Sakala, in south-western central Estonia, was one of the major ancient Estonian lands, with hillforts at Viljandi and Lehola. It bordered the Livonians and Latgalians to the south, with whom it traded and fought, and appears in detail in the Livonian Chronicle of Henry from the early 13th century.
sakala.r: Like other Estonian counties, Sakala was led by elders who commanded the levies of its parishes and negotiated with neighbours. Lembitu of Lehola organised alliances across Estonia and sought help from Novgorod and Pskov against the Germans, an unusually wide coalition for the time.
sakala.e: Lembitu was killed at the Battle of St Matthew's Day near Viljandi in 1217, and the crusaders took Viljandi. An uprising in 1223 briefly expelled them, but Sakala was reconquered by 1224 and passed to the Livonian Brothers of the Sword, later the Livonian Order, which built Fellin castle there.

sordones.t: People of the Roussillon plain beneath the eastern Pyrenees, whose town Ruscino gave the region its name.
sordones.o: Known only from Greek and Roman writers such as Avienus, Pomponius Mela and Pliny, the Sordones held the coastal plain around Ruscino (Château-Roussillon, near Perpignan). Their culture had strong Iberian ties, and their land lay on the coastal route between Iberia and Gaul.
sordones.r: Livy reports that in 218 BCE Gallic chiefs gathered at Ruscino to decide whether to let Hannibal pass on his march to Italy, and he won them over with gifts. Excavations at Ruscino show a hilltop settlement with storage silos and imported Greek and Italian goods.
sordones.e: After 121 BCE the area was absorbed into the Roman province of Gallia Narbonensis. Ruscino became a small Roman town with a forum before declining, and its name survives in Roussillon.

state-of-damascus.t: One of the states into which France divided Syria in 1920, built around Damascus and later merged into a unified Syrian state.
state-of-damascus.o: After defeating the Arab Kingdom of Syria at Maysalun in July 1920, the French high commissioner Henri Gouraud divided Syria into several states to weaken Arab nationalism. The State of Damascus, created in September 1920, covered Damascus, Homs, Hama and the south.
state-of-damascus.r: The state had a local government under a governor, the first being Haqqi al-Azm, with French advisers holding real authority. It was the centre of nationalist politics and resentment at the division of Syria. In 1922 it joined the Syrian Federation with the State of Aleppo and the Alawite State.
state-of-damascus.e: At the end of 1924 France dissolved the federation and merged the states of Damascus and Aleppo into the State of Syria, which took effect in January 1925.

sultanate-of-moheli.t: The smallest Comoran sultanate, founded by a Merina prince and ruled by Queen Djoumbe Fatima before falling under France.
sultanate-of-moheli.o: Around 1830 Ramanetaka, a Merina prince and governor who had fled Madagascar, seized control of Moheli (Mwali) and set himself up as sultan with the Muslim name Abderremane, displacing the island's earlier rulers.
sultanate-of-moheli.r: After Ramanetaka's death in 1842 his young daughter Djoumbe Fatima became queen. Her long reign saw rival French and British influence and a controversial plantation lease to a French trader, while the small island lived from fishing, farming and trade with Zanzibar. Islam and Swahili culture shaped court life at Fomboni.
sultanate-of-moheli.e: France imposed a protectorate in 1886, and the last queen, Salima Machamba, abdicated before the island was annexed and attached to the Colony of Mayotte and Dependencies. Moheli is now part of the Union of the Comoros.

second-taifa-of-valencia.t: Valencia's short independence under its qadi after the Almoravid collapse, a prelude to the rise of Ibn Mardanish, the Wolf King.
second-taifa-of-valencia.o: In 1145 the notables of Valencia expelled the Almoravid governor and recognised their qadi, Marwan ibn Abd al-Aziz, as ruler, part of the wave of urban revolts that ended Almoravid rule in eastern al-Andalus.
second-taifa-of-valencia.r: The regime rested on the qadi's prestige and the support of the city's elite, but it lacked troops. Real military power in the east lay with commanders such as Ibn Iyad and, after him, Muhammad ibn Mardanish, who soon pushed the qadi aside.
second-taifa-of-valencia.e: By 1147 Ibn Mardanish had taken control of Valencia and joined it to his realm, the Second Taifa of Murcia, which held out against the Almohads until 1172.

sertorian-state.t: The breakaway Roman regime of Quintus Sertorius, who with Iberian allies held most of Hispania against the Senate for nearly a decade.
sertorian-state.o: Quintus Sertorius, a supporter of Marius, was driven from Hispania by Sulla's forces but returned in 80 BCE at the invitation of the Lusitanians. Combining Roman exiles with Lusitanian and Celtiberian warriors, he defeated Sulla's generals and by 77 BCE controlled much of Hispania Citerior and Ulterior.
sertorian-state.r: Sertorius ran a rival Roman state with its own senate of exiles and magistrates, while winning Iberian loyalty through fair treatment and personal charisma, aided by a white fawn said to bring him divine messages. At Osca he founded a school where sons of Iberian nobles learned Latin and Greek, partly as hostages. He allied with Mithridates VI of Pontus and beat Pompey at Lauron in 76 BCE.
sertorian-state.e: Worn down by Metellus Pius and Pompey, his alliance frayed. In 73 or 72 BCE he was murdered at a banquet by his lieutenant Marcus Perperna, whom Pompey soon defeated and executed. Hispania returned to Senate rule.

sabines.t: Italic people of the hills north-east of Rome, central to Roman foundation legends, who were absorbed by Rome in the early 3rd century BCE.
sabines.o: The Sabines lived in the central Apennines and the hill country between the Tiber and the Aniene from the early 1st millennium BCE. Ancient writers saw them as the parent stock of several Sabellian peoples, such as the Samnites and Picentes, who were said to have left Sabine land in 'sacred springs' of migration.
sabines.r: Sabine society was rural, made up of villages and small towns such as Cures, Reate, Nursia and Amiternum, with a reputation in Roman eyes for austere virtue. They spoke an Osco-Umbrian language known only from glosses. In Roman legend the abduction of the Sabine women led to joint rule between Romulus and the Sabine king Titus Tatius, and Rome's second king Numa Pompilius came from Cures. The Claudii were said to descend from Attus Clausus, who moved to Rome around 504 BCE.
sabines.e: Manius Curius Dentatus conquered the Sabines in 290 BCE. They received citizenship without the vote, and full citizenship in 268 BCE, an early and complete absorption into the Roman state. Their land was later part of Augustus's Regio IV, and the name survives in the Sabina district north of Rome.

southern-tang.t: The largest and most cultured of the southern Ten Kingdoms, ruled from Nanjing by a house that claimed Tang descent and ended with the poet-king Li Yu.
southern-tang.o: Xu Zhigao, adopted son of the regent Xu Wen, took the throne of Wu (Ten Kingdoms) in 937. In 939 he took the name Li Bian, claimed descent from the Tang imperial family and renamed his state Tang, ruling from Jinling (Nanjing).
southern-tang.r: Southern Tang held the wealthy lower Yangtze and Jiangxi. Under Li Jing it conquered Min (Ten Kingdoms) in 945 and Ma Chu in 951 but could not hold them. Its court patronised painting, calligraphy and lyric poetry, and its paper and ink were famous. In 958 Later Zhou took its lands between the Huai and Yangtze, and it became a tributary of the north.
southern-tang.e: Li Yu, a celebrated writer of song lyrics, tried to appease the Song Dynasty, but Song armies took Jinling in 975. He was taken to Kaifeng, where his poems lamenting his lost kingdom were composed, and died in 978, reputedly poisoned.
